Are some pleasures more noble than others? Do immoral people just have bad luck? Is monogamy unethical? Is the existence of evil a problem for belief in God? Should we try to become immortal? Is everything we do ultimately motivated by self-interest? Is it immoral to have children? Are there good arguments against objective morality? Should we use genetic therapies to increase intelligence? Is it morally permissible to select your child's race? Does free will require the ability to do otherwise? Do our lives have meaning? Mexican Soul - D id you know you can make the best guacamole you’ve ever tasted without using avocado? Or that tortillas and tamales can be made with potato? Through years of research, exploration and cooking in restaurants around the globe, chef Santiago Lastra has discovered a secret: you can make incredible Mexican food without having to hunt down specific ingredients or buy traditional produce that has lost its freshness by the time it lands in your kitchen. Mexican flavor can be unlocked anywhere in the world, with almost any ingredient, and this book is the key to finding it. Get ready to discover Mexican Soul: A New Style of Cooking .

ff498187-2091-4f15-88c4-01a7bf9ce7bd: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

2acd05f8-44b5-4a1f-8dac-81d21bd039fe: The Science of Longing: What would make you believe the impossible? · What happens when the desire to know becomes inseparable from the desire for something to be true? We like to imagine reason as solid ground, but grief, love, memory, and loss can make the boundaries between evidence, belief, obsession, and hope much harder to see. In their debut novels, Scott Lambridis and Yance Wyatt explore characters confronting realities that strain the explanations available to them. Their conversation will move among psychology, science, faith, mythology, and the impossible to ask what makes a belief reasonable, where skepticism becomes its own kind of certainty, and whether emotion distorts inquiry or gives it urgency. At stake is a deeply human question: when ordinary explanations fail us, what are we willing to believe in order to keep making sense of the world? Scott Lambridis writes literary speculative fiction about the stories people rely on to make sense of the world. He studied neurobiology before earning an MFA in Fiction from San Francisco State University. His fiction explores belief, consciousness, trauma, and the strange places where psychology, folklore, and love begin to overlap. Before publishing his debut novel, St. Ulphia’s Dead, Scott toured with a progressive rock band, founded an independent press and literary performance series, tended a forty-acre olive farm, and read a book from every country in the world. Yance Wyatt studied fiction at the University of Cambridge and the University of Southern California, where he has gone on to serve as professor of writing and director of the Writing Center. As fiction editor with The Blue Mountain Review, he seeks to acquire the best new stories from the South. His own stories have appeared in dozens of nationally circulated literary journals and received several Pushcart Prize nominations. The Watersmith is his first novel.

88978a3b-0afd-4b06-93fd-342eb547ebb7: 🎬 What does a TV show sound like when it wants to feel like a movie? Television music used to sit politely in the background. Today, it can carry whole worlds. From the sweeping string covers of Bridgerton to the chilling minimalism of Severance, scores now shape what we feel, who we trust, and what we dread long before a character says a word. Join Rebecca Nisco, Composer and Pixar Associate Music & Sound Editor, for a look at how TV scoring has become more cinematic and more serialized. Through examples from Bridgerton, The Queen's Gambit, Severance, and Succession, Rebecca will show how music builds atmosphere, develops characters, and drives storytelling. You will also hear how a distinctive musical world becomes part of a series' identity, and why music plays such an important role in the television we love. Bring your ears and your favorite theme song. 🎻 📵 A No-Phone Lecture 📵 This event is a special one: we are asking attendees not to use their phones during the duration of the event (7-9pm). After you check in, we will ask you to turn your phone off and slip it into an envelope provided at the door. a3b1d4e4-ee3f-4310-a2c1-5155585b485f: Join us on Wednesday, November 11 at 7pm when Kelly Grace Thomas celerates the release of her collection, Future Tense, at 9th Ave! Featuring Kim Addonizio, Tracey Knapp, and Yaccaira Salvatierra Free to Attend, Please RSVP Or Watch on YouTube Live at the Link Below https://youtube.com/live/oSL8kWYaCoQ?feature=share Praise for Future Tense “A beautiful meditation on the slow, aching, and sometimes miraculous state of intertwined grief...”—Hanif Abdurraqib, author of There's Always This Year "In eclectic structures, whether careful tercets or sprawling fragments, Thomas ricochets between loss and desire until they blend..."—Shira Erlichman, author of Odes to Lithium "....Future Tense learns how deeply love is entangled with endurance. The poems widen to hold grief and arrival in the same hands, writing toward care, astonishment, and gratitude, the wisdom of waiting and loss."—Diannely Antigua, author of Good Monster About Future Tense Reckoning with infertility, adoption, and love under pressure, Kelly Grace Thomas’s Future Tense is a searing memoir-in-verse about a woman’s fight to become a mother while losing her own. Thomas spends three years trying for a child who never arrives. As she struggles with infertility, her mother is dying of Stage IV uterine cancer, and the desire for a child turns urgent—a countdown. As her mother’s health deteriorates, time narrows, pressure builds, and the clock refuses to slow. As her marriage strains and the world remakes itself without her, Thomas refuses to give up. The fertility clinic is the coldest place on earth; still, she keeps going—through years of medical gaslighting, IVF consults, mounting debt, and backhanded blame—finally welcoming her daughter through adoption just months before her mother’s death. Intimate and unflinching, Future Tense interrogates the intertwined joys and griefs of womanhood and motherhood—and how biology can sometimes turn against us. Thomas approaches illness and loss with clarity and care, writing with a generosity that welcomes readers in. Despite their brevity, these poems refuse despair, finding meaning and connection even in the hardest seasons of life. About Kelly Grace Thomas Kelly Grace Thomas, poet, writer, and coach, is the author of Future Tense and Boat Burned. She is the winner of the Jane Underwood Poetry Prize and the Neil Postman Award for Metaphor from Rattle. Kelly’s poems have appeared or are forthcoming in: The Sun, The Adroit Journal, 32 Poems, Los Angeles Review, Sixth Finch, and elsewhere. She holds an MFA in Creative Writing from Randolph College and live in Benicia, where she coaches poetry online. www.kellygracethomas.com About the Readers Kim Addonizio’s most recent poetry collection is Exit Opera (W.W.Norton). She is the author of eight other poetry collections, two novels, two story collections, and two books on writing poetry, The Poet’s Companion (with Dorianne Laux) and Ordinary Genius, as well as a memoir-in-essays, Bukowski in a Sundress: Confessions from a Writing Life. Addonizio’s work has been honored with fellowships from the NEA and Guggenheim Foundation, and her collection Tell Me was a finalist for the National Book Award. She lives in Oakland, CA and teaches poetry workshops on Zoom. Find her online at https://www.kimaddonizio.com . Tracey Knapp's second collection, Swerve, was released from Pine Row Press in Spring 2026. Her first full-length collection of poems, Mouth, won the 42 Miles Press Poetry Award and was published in 2015. Tracey has received awards and scholarships from La Romita School of Art in Terni, Italy, the Tin House Writers’ Workshop, and the Dorothy Sargent Rosenberg Poetry Fund. Her work has appeared in Academy of American Poets Poem-a-Day, Best New Poets, Poetry Daily, Rattle, Five Points, New Ohio Review and elsewhere. She has been nominated for Best of the Net and two Pushcart prizes. Originally from New York’s Hudson Valley, Tracey lives in the Bay Area of California. Born in Los Ángeles, California, Yaccaira Salvatierra is a poet, translator, and dedicated educator teaching for over 20 years while raising her two sons as a single parent. Her debut collection, Sons of Salt (BOA, 2024) was deemed one of the "Best Books for Adults 2024" by the New York Public Library. She earned her BA at the University of California at Santa Cruz, an MA at San José State University, and an MFA at Randolph College. She received the Dorrit Sibley Award for Poetry and the Puerto del Sol Poetry Prize. She has been awarded the Lucille Clifton Memorial Scholarship as a fellow at the Community of Writers Workshop, and scholarships for the Napa Valley Writers’ Conference, Bread Loaf Translator’s Conference, and Macondo. She is an organizer for the San Francisco International Flor y Canto Literary Festival and lives in Oakland, CA, where she teaches literacy and poetry to youth.
a4a8e4c8-3f38-4382-844c-b32ec523d592: What would make you believe the impossible? · What happens when the desire to know becomes inseparable from the desire for something to be true? We like to imagine reason as solid ground, but grief, love, memory, and loss can make the boundaries between evidence, belief, obsession, and hope much harder to see. In their debut novels, Scott Lambridis and Yance Wyatt explore characters confronting realities that strain the explanations available to them. Their conversation will move between psychology, science, faith, mythology, and the impossible to ask what makes a belief reasonable, where skepticism becomes its own kind of certainty, and whether emotion distorts inquiry or gives it urgency. At stake is a deeply human question: when ordinary explanations fail us, what are we willing to believe in order to keep making sense of the world? Scott Lambridis writes literary speculative fiction about the stories people rely on to make sense of the world. He studied neurobiology before earning an MFA in Fiction from San Francisco State University. His fiction explores belief, consciousness, trauma, and the strange places where psychology, folklore, and love begin to overlap. Before publishing his debut novel, St. Ulphia’s Dead, Scott toured with a progressive rock band, founded an independent press and literary performance series, tended a forty-acre olive farm, and read a book from every country in the world. He lives in Bellingham, Washington, with his family. More at scottlambridis.com . Yance Wyatt was born and raised in Nashville, Tennessee. He studied fiction at the University of Cambridge and the University of Southern California, where he has gone on to serve as professor of writing and director of the Writing Center. As fiction editor with The Blue Mountain Review, he seeks to acquire the best new stories from the South. His own stories have appeared in dozens of nationally circulated literary journals and received several Pushcart Prize nominations. The Watersmith is his first novel. Visit him @yancewyatt or www.yancewyatt.com .

d2b1d848-edcb-4763-a03a-a2a11fb9067e: Step into the magical world of ELF with this captivating oral history, written by beloved comedian and actor Andy Richter, who watched the on-set shenanigans unfold before his very eyes, and featuring a foreword by Will Ferrell!! Ever since Elf hit theaters, audiences around the world have fallen in love with the story of Buddy, the charming (and oversized) "elf" with a heart of gold. But what most people don’t know is that when the screenplay first hit Hollywood, no studio was willing to touch it. How, then, did such a risky gamble turn into one of the most beloved Christmas classics of all time? In this laugh-out-loud oral history, comedian and co-star Andy Richter goes on a mission to find out by reconnecting with the very people who brought this festive vision to life. Through exclusive interviews, hilarious anecdotes, and heartfelt reflections with key players like Will Ferrell, Zooey Deschanel, director Jon Favreau, and many others, Andy ultimately unwraps the story of how a quirky holiday film about a human raised by elves became such an enduring cultural phenomenon. Packed with never-before-seen photos, behind-the-scenes secrets, a foreword by Buddy himself (aka Will Ferrell), and a sprinkle of festive fun, this book is the perfect gift for anyone who believes in the magic of Christmas—and knows that the best way to spread holiday cheer is by singing loud for all to hear. Andy Richter is a comedian, actor, writer, and host. He's best known for his many years as Conan O’Brien’s collaborator and sidekick. He has appeared in numerous television shows and films, some of them quite good. He is also the host of the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show , and enjoyed a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars . He's based in Los Angeles. e5b9699f-a6c6-4697-bd4a-829fba8d4851: 🔌 What happens when a cyberattack stops being virtual and starts turning off the lights? Critical infrastructure has become a domain of conflict between nation-states. Before a single shot is fired on a battlefield, an adversary can seek advantage by disrupting the systems a nation relies on to function: the rail lines and ports that move troops and supplies, the water systems that sustain our cities, the power grid that enables modern life. In this talk, Dr. Nate Gleason, Program Leader for the Cyber and Infrastructure Resilience Program at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, explores why the old strategy of building a strong perimeter and hoping to keep adversaries out is no longer enough. Sophisticated attackers will eventually find a way in, so Gleason and his team are developing what they call immune infrastructure: a layered approach that combines protection, detection, response, and resilience to prevent a cyber intrusion from becoming a physical consequence. Gleason will discuss the technologies being built to keep essential systems running through an attack, and how artificial intelligence is reshaping both sides of this escalating competition. ⚡ 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? 0009ec6a-bddd-4316-9873-62bf8df4a704: (Please do not bring infants to the show) Born into a radical theater company, Joyful Raven was tasked from the tender age of 5 with the daunting mission to save the world from impending doom… using theater. Forced into animal-print unitards and political positions long before she was a consenting adult, she never had a fighting chance at anything resembling a normal life. You think your parents were embarrassing? Did you have to sing about salmon sex on stage, in a unitard, at 12 years old… WITH your parents? I didn’t think so. In an attempt to heal her hippie trauma, she runs away from home to seek solace in the arms of a spiritual teacher… and accidentally finds herself in the yoga-to-fascism pipeline. Can she save herself? Can she save the world… using theater?! Or does she have to choose? Blending standup, drag, storytelling, & clown, Raven takes audiences on a dystopian and hilarious romp through the looking glass. Joyful Raven is an award-winning actor, director, and “story midwife” known for her powerful and thought-provoking solo shows, where she tackles thorny social issues with humor, heart, and nuance. Born into an iconic political theater family, she has been devising original work for over 20 years. Her first solo comedy, Tales of a Sexual Tomboy, was dubbed “…one of the funniest shows now on display on Bay Area stages” by the SF Chronicle, won Best of the Fringe at the 2016 San Francisco International Fringe Festival, and enjoyed an Off-Broadway run in 2017. Her latest solo show, Breed or Bust, was nominated for Best Comedy at the 2022 Hollywood Fringe Festival, critically acclaimed at the 2023 Edinburgh Fringe, where it won an Offie (OffWestEnd Award), and went on to have an extended run at The Marsh, where it received a Critics’ Pick in the SF Chronicle. She co-founded the award-winning theater company Rococo Risqué and co-authored four plays for the Prize of Hope-winning company Human Nature. As an actor, she has appeared in numerous stage and film projects, including Odyssey Works, the film The Pursuit of Happyness alongside Will Smith, and Spring Awakening, directed by Stafford Arima. Joyful holds an MFA in Dramatic Art from the University of California, Davis, and teaches solo performance and storytelling at Berkeley Rep School of Theatre, The Marsh, and her own studio in Berkeley. Dara Kosberg is a storyteller, comedian, and writer. She debuted her solo storytelling show “Homecoming” to sold-out shows in NYC, LA, Atlanta and Chicago. She’s a Moth StorySlam winner and has performed at San Francisco’s Punch Line Comedy Club and Brooklyn’s Union Hall. As part of the Reimagine End of Life arts festival in SF and NYC, she’s produced and performed in comedy shows about grief and loss that demonstrate the healing power of humor. Piece Description – Homecoming Dara’s 15 minute piece is an excerpt of “Homecoming”, her solo show that was recently nominated for the Comedic Theatre Award and StageCrafts’ Freeway Circuit Award at the 2026 Hollywood Fringe Festival. A dark comedy, “Homecoming” begins when Dara is studying art in Australia when she gets that call— her mom is dying, and she has to come home. Suddenly, their already difficult mother/daughter relationship becomes a lot more complicated. How do you make amends with a dead mom? What follows is a winding journey through the awkward, painful, unexpectedly hilarious process of finding yourself again after loss. Directed by David Ford, Artist-in- Residence at The Marsh. 4062dd46-ca7d-47af-b089-284e2b45f3fd: One of today’s premier jazz drummers · "The Groove Master", Herlin Riley is widely considered one of the best drummers in any genre of music performing today. The longtime drummer for the legendary Ahmad Jamal and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra now leads two groups, his quintet and the New Orleans Groove Masters featuring himself, Jason Marsalis, and Shannon Powell. Herlin’s most recent album, Perpetual Optimism, reunites the quintet of rising stars that Riley assembled for his Mack Avenue Records debut, New Direction. Since the release of that acclaimed album, all four of Riley’s bandmates – trumpeter Bruce Harris, saxophonist Godwin Louis, pianist Emmet Cohen, and bassist Russell Hall – have been making major waves across the modern jazz scene, attesting to the master drummer’s Art Blakey-like ear for talent and sage musical guidance. Herlin Riley's source of strength comes from his faith in God, his wife of four decades, and his family of five children and 10 grandchildren; his lifelong home in New Orleans, the creative community that surrounds it, and his positive approach to life and music. His roots in the church are also vital, shining through in the congregational claps that help establish the celebratory spirit that is showcased in the album opener “Rush Hour.” He also relies on his musical family, including his long-established ties with Wynton Marsalis and the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra. Riley’s connection to the Marsalis dynasty traces back a generation earlier, to family patriarch and fellow lifelong New Orleanian Ellis Marsalis. It was while performing with Ellis at the annual New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival in a trio with bassist Reginald Veal that Riley first caught the ear of Wynton, who invited both members of his father’s rhythm section to join him, launching a vital relationship that’s now lasted more than three decades. Riley pays homage to his mentor on the closing track of Perpetual Optimism, the funky arrangement of Ellis Marsalis’ composition “Twelve’s It.” In the quintet’s lively rendition, the tune is not just a cover but a tribute, as Riley intones a short ode to passing the torch that refers to the elder Marsalis as “a great musician who taught a whole lot of fellows.” Another Crescent City icon, the late singer, pianist, songwriter, and producer Allen Toussaint, was the motivator behind Riley’s other vocal turn on the album, a gritty take on Willie Dixon’s blues classic “Wang Dang Doodle.” Toussaint stopped in to hear Riley play at a New Orleans club and heard the drummer’s 5/4 arrangement of the familiar standard. “He was really impressed,” Riley recalls. “He said, ‘Wow, man, I’ve heard ‘Wang Dang Doodle’ a thousand times, but I’ve never heard it performed in 5 before. You should record that.’ A few months later, he passed away, so I recorded the tune to pay homage to the wishes of the great Allen Toussaint.” Though he conveys vivid emotion in his voice, Riley stops short of calling himself a singer. His willingness to step to the mic comes from advice he was given by New Orleans vocal great Germaine Bazzle. “She’s a very elegant and regal lady, but when she’s performing, she scats, rolls her shoulders, dances, and really engages in the music with honesty and passion,” says Riley. When he asked her how she reconciled those two extremes, Bazzle told him, “’ You have to allow yourself to become emotionally naked when you’re on the bandstand.’ When she said that, a light bulb went off in my head. I’m not a singer, but I just do what I do, and I have the audacity to be uninhibited.” The same can be said for Riley’s work behind the kit, where he leads his stellar band with infectious enthusiasm and bristling swing. His “Be There When I Get There” captures the anticipation and excitement of rushing to an eagerly awaited appointment, whether a romantic rendezvous, a gathering of friends, or a night of music. The brisk “Borders Without Lines” comes from the pen of Riley’s Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra bandmate Victor Goines, while the classic “You Don’t Know What Love Is” becomes a sultry simmer, highlighted by Harris’ mournful, muted trumpet. The title track is the rare Riley original composed in a major key, and its sunny disposition perfectly communicates his unflagging hopefulness. The lovely “Touched,” featuring Louis’ achingly lyrical alto, recalls a tender moment with the drummer’s mother before she passed away. “I was in her room in her last days, and she rubbed my head. I’m a grown man, but I felt like an innocent child. There’s a special love wrapped in the touch of a mother of every living creature. That special euphoria only comes from her.” The bittersweet “Wings and Roots” looks to the next generation, referring to Riley’s philosophy of raising children: “You have to root them in good values and fundamental characteristics, but once they get to be a certain age, you have to give them the wings to be free, to go out and be themselves.” Finally, “Stella By Starlight” is another nod to the American Songbook, taken at a graceful midtempo pace with Cohen’s deft touch over Riley’s sensitive brushwork. In the end, Riley hopes that the music of Perpetual Optimism helps spread the upbeat manifesto that he’s chosen to live by. “I always look forward, no matter what happens in life. If you’re grieving or faced with an emotional challenge, keep in mind: If you’re still breathing, there’s a chance that you can overcome and thrive. Commit yourself to PERPETUAL OPTIMISM!”

62f99c79-993d-43c5-bb57-55a12f511478: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com

7bec954a-e2f6-4b53-bc73-956ed8deccff: Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Presented by Fort Mason Art Points Of Departure is a new series of immersive live events celebrating the spectrum of Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture (FMCAC) as a place for innovation and discovery, a personal port of embarkation for its community, and a window on the world. Each program celebrates the vibrant past, present, and future of FMCAC as it charts a course toward its 50th anniversary in 2027. Points Of Departure is curated by Brad Rosenstein, Associate Curator of Public Programs. Two Points Of Departure Fall 2026 Events Happen in The Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor Program 2 CIRCUS BY THE BAY Panel conversation and live performances Tuesday, October 13, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Cowell Theater, Pier 2/Gateway Pavilion, FMCAC , RESERVE SPACE Pickle Family Circus at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture Lively Arts Festival 1978. Photo: Terry Lorant In the 1970s, San Francisco became an epicenter of the emerging new American circus – an intimate one-ring model that spurned animal acts and focused on traditional skills of juggling, clowning, acrobatics, and aerial work, all filtered through a countercultural vaudevillian sensibility. This “not-so-big-top” was pioneered by such local companies as the Pickle Family Circus and its later incarnation, the New Pickle Circus, which performed annually at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture, and longtime FMCAC residents Make*A*Circus. This movement spawned a stream of Bay Area talents that spread their influence from Cirque du Soleil and Broadway to movies, and TV, an impact which resonates to this day. Join us for a magical evening celebrating this uniquely San Francisco history through a conversation with some of its leading lights, all veterans of Pickle Family Circus and the New Pickle Circus: performer/writer/director Gypsy Snider , trapeze artist/choreographer/director Shana Carroll , clown/writer/teacher Jeff Raz , and artistic director/choreographer Tandy Beal . The program includes rare archival photos and video, and live performances by Unique Derique ( Prescott Circus ), Chloe Somers Walier ( Dear San Francisco ), Elise Hing ( Circus Bella ), and performers from San Francisco Youth Circus ( SFYC ), Circus Center ’s pre-professional youth program. SFYC is led by Performance Coach Dominic Cruz , a 7 Fingers/ Dear San Francisco alum. (performers subject to change). Program 3 LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION Panel conversation and rare performance video Thursday, November 12, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center or Arts & Culture , RESERVE SPACE LEFT TO RIGHT: LIFE ON THE WATER’s Bill Talen , Ellen Sebastian , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert with a model of the Bayfront Theatre remodel 1987. LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW) was an extraordinary presenting and producing organization based at Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture for seven seasons between 1986-1993. Centered in its own custom-designed space (now the Bayfront Theatre), the company was dedicated to presenting artists who originated their own work and committed to a blend of experimental and traditional stage forms, political statement, and cultural diversity. It became nationally renowned for its pioneering showcases of solo theater work by such luminaries as Spalding Gray and Karen Finley as well as co-producing the annual Solo Mio Festival. LOTW’s presentations also ranged from music, dance, screenings, and workshops to ongoing programs such as Latino Theatre Project, Earth Drama Lab, and AsianImprov aRts (AIR). This special evening reunites LOTW’s founding directors Ellen Sebastian Chang , Bill Talen , Leonard Pitt , and Joe Lambert on their former stage for a sparkling conversation about the company’s groundbreaking work, which includes their own creations ranging from Pitt’s “avant mime” theater Not for Real and Sebastian’s epic The Sanctified Church to Talen’s biting satires such as Political Wife . The program includes never-before-seen archival video of some of LOTW’s most celebrated productions. Past Programs Program 1 TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Film screening and panel conversation Thursday, September 24, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m. Bayfront Theatre, Building B, Third Floor, Fort Mason Center For Arts & Culture (FMCAC) , RESERVE SPACE TELL THEM WE WERE HERE Artist Alicia McCarthy Tell Them We Were Here (2021), a film by Griff Williams and Keelan Williams , chronicles visual/multidisciplinary artists currently living and working in the San Francisco Bay Area and how they extend the historical legacy of Bay Area creativity, activism, and community. Reflecting the spirit of FMCAC and its vibrant connection to local art and artists, the film centers the idea of art as a reflection of the place from which it emerges and helps to define the unique character of the Bay Area scene over the past 25 years. The film follows the work of Sadie Barnette , Amy Franceschini ( Futurefarmers ), Jim Goldberg , Tucker Nichols , Lynn Hershman Leeson , Alicia McCarthy , Nigel Poor ( Ear Hustle ), and M ichael Swaine , a select group of artists who have chosen a less-worn path. It touches on the disappearance of cultural communities due to gentrification and economic instability, while reminding us of art’s power to transform and how vital creative communities are to healthy societies and political change. The screening is followed by a panel discussion with director Griff Williams , artists Amy Franceschini and Tucker Nichols , and curator René de Guzman (all featured in the film), exploring how the local art scene has continued to evolve in the five years since the film’s premiere. All Fort Mason Art programs are generously supported by San Francisco Grants for The Arts, the FMCAC Board of Directors, and individual contributions to the Fort Mason Fund. PANELISTS & PERFORMERS PANELISTS TELL THEM WE WERE HERE : Griff Williams is an American painter, publisher and gallerist. In 1993 he founded Gallery 16 and the pioneering fine art printmaking workshop Urban Digital Color in San Francisco. The exhibition and publishing program has worked with hundreds of artists including Lynn Hershman Leeson, William Kentridge, Deborah Oropallo, Jim Isermann, bell hooks, Rex Ray, Margaret Kilgallen, Mark Grotjahn, Paul Sietsema, Arturo Herrera, Michelle Grabner, and Ari Marcopoulos. Williams has also designed and published dozens of acclaimed books with the Gallery 16 Editions imprint. His paintings have been exhibited in galleries and museums including the San Diego Museum of Art, the Crocker Art Museum in Sacramento, and the San Jose Museum of Art . His work has been reviewed in Art in America , Flash Art , and ARTnews . He co-directed Tell Them We Were Here with his son, Keelan Williams , a filmmaker based in Los Angeles. René de Guzman is a longtime Bay Area curator, artist, and arts consultant. He was one of the founding curators at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts as Visual Arts Curator and Director of Visual Arts, serving from 1993-2007, and subsequently served as the Senior Curator of Art and Director of Exhibition Strategy at the Oakland Museum of California from 2007-21. He also served as Deputy Director for Programs and Engagement at Headlands Center for the Arts , overseeing artist residencies and public programs. For more than three decades, he has developed innovative and popular exhibitions for a wide public and is currently Co-Director of Art + Water in San Francisco. Amy Franceschini is an artist whose work facilitates encounter, exchange, and tactile forms of inquiry by calling into question the “certainties” of a given time or place where a work is situated. In 1995, Franceschini founded Futurefarmers as a collaborative platform to consider the social, political, and environmental organization of space. Futurefarmers use various media to deconstruct systems to visualize and understand their intrinsic logics; food systems, public transportation, education … Through this disassembly they find new narratives and reconfigurations that form alternatives to the principles that once dominated these systems. Franceschini received her BFA in Photography from San Francisco State University and an MFA from Stanford University. She has taught in the visual arts graduate programs at California College of the Arts in San Francisco and Stanford University and in the Master of Eco-Social Design at the Free University in Bolzano, Italy. She is a 2009 Guggenheim Fellow, a 2019 Rome Prize Fellow and a 2017 recipient of the Herb Alpert Award for Visual Arts. Tucker Nichols is an artist based in Northern California. His work has been featured at the Drawing Center in New York, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Denver Art Museum, Den Frie Museum in Copenhagen, and the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. A show of his sculpture, Almost Everything On The Table , was recently on view at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum. His drawings have been published in McSweeney’s , The Thing Quarterly , The New Yorker , and the Op-Ed pages of The New York Times . He is co-author of the books, Crabtree (with Jon Nichols) and This Bridge Will Not Be Gray (with Dave Eggers). Flowers for Sick People , his ongoing multimedia project, was featured on the PBS Newshour and the subject of an exhibition at SFMOMA, Close to Home: Creativity in Crisis , is an exhibition highlighting seven local artists’ responses to the pandemic. He is represented by ZieherSmith in New York and Gallery 16 in San Francisco. CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Gypsy Snider is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , now celebrating its fifth anniversary at the city’s historic Club Fugazi. As co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers , she wrote and directed SisterS , Réversible, Intersection , Amuse , Un D i a , Traces , and Loft . She has choreographed televised feature performances for America’s Got Talent and Her Majesty’s Royal Variety Performance . In 2013, working with director Diane Paulus on a new vision of Pippin , she created choreography and wove circus into the revival of the Broadway musical, earning her a Drama Desk Award and an Outer Critics Circle Award. Snider began her circus career at the age of four when her parents founded The Pickle Family Circus. She grew up touring the West Coast with the company. In 2002, while in her hometown of San Francisco, she wrote and directed for The New Pickle Circus a show entitled Circumstance , which premiered at FMCAC’s Cowell Theater. Snider is also a guest teacher and guest director at the National Circus School of Montreal. Shana Carroll is co-artistic director of Dear San Francisco , and co-founding artistic director of The 7 Fingers . Since the latter’s inception in 2002, Shana has directed, written, and created choreography for a dozen or so of their touring and/or resident shows, including Passagers , Cuisine & Confessions , Séquence 8 , and Traces . in 2024 Carroll was co-choreographer and Circus Designer for Water For Elephants on Broadway, for which she received the Chita Rivera Award for Best Choreography, as well as Tony, Drama Desk, and Outer Critics Circles nominations in the same category. Carroll has frequently collaborated with Cirque du Soleil , most recently as co-director of their first show on ice, Crystal , and previously as acrobatic designer and choreographer of Paramour (Broadway) and Iris (Los Angeles), and as director/choreographer of their performance at the 2012 Academy Awards. Originally from Berkeley, CA, and daughter of beloved San Francisco columnist Jon Carroll, Shana began her career as a trapeze artist with San Francisco’s Pickle Family Circus and went on to a 20-year career in the air with Cirque du Soleil and many others before co-founding The 7 Fingers. Jeff Raz has performed nationally and internationally for decades, starring in the Pickle Family Circus, Cirque du Soleil’s Corteo , Make*A*Circus, and many other circuses and theaters. Jeff is also a playwright, director, teacher, producer and has authored four books inspired by his career. Over the years he has also co-founded six arts organizations and worked globally as a communications and leadership consultant. Tandy Beal is a performer, director, choreographer, writer, teacher, and … dreamer. An off-the-map career includes: directing Pickle Family Circus for 10 years; touring four continents with Tandy Beal & Co.; writing/directing VIVA for the Moscow Circus in Japan; a show for NASA’s SETI project with Carl Sagan; projects with Lou Harrison, Frank Zappa, John Adams, and decades of projects with Bobby McFerrin, Art Lande, and Jon Scoville; choreographing opera, MTV, ballet; corporate shows (LucasFilms, SF 49ers, MCI, Coca-Cola, Pixar, Oracle+); acting off-Broadway; dancing for the Shah of Iran with Alwin Nikolais in Tehran; guest performances with Atlanta Ballet, Momix, Remy Charlip and in Europe, with Carolyn Carlson; creating what Dance Magazine said was the first contemporary dance/circus Nutcracker . Her life and work are featured in two books, The Pickle Clowns and Living Happily Ever After . She has received awards from AFI, CAC, NEA, Packard, and Hewlett +. Her natural habitat is the Santa Cruz mountains where she lives with longtime co-conspirator, Jon Scoville. PANELISTS LIFE ON THE WATER: A REUNION : Ellen Sebastian Chang is a distinguished multidisciplinary director, dramaturge, writer, and arts educator with a career spanning 50 years, dedicated to advocating for human rights and understanding through the creative arts. She has collaborated with a diverse array of artists and art forms: theater, opera, dance, radio, film and installation. Sebastian Chang commenced her career as a lighting technician and designer before making her debut as a director and writer in 1982 with Your Place Is No Longer With Us , an immersive play staged in private homes about a biracial girl. She co-founded LIFE ON THE WATER (LOTW), a notable producing organization in San Francisco, and served as its co-artistic director. During her time at LOTW she created The Sanctified Church with Luisah Teisch, later renamed Sanctified with Esther Scott, No Trace of the Blonde with Holly Hughes, and Janie Geiser, FACE with Bob Ernst, Artis Fountaine, NAO, and Debora Iyall. She has been the creative director and teaching artist for The World As It Could Be Human Rights Education Program, utilizing the arts to deepen understanding of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and inspire activism across generations. Beyond her work in theater, she co-owned the award-winning FuseBOX restaurant in West Oakland created with Chef Sunhui Chang. She has received numerous grants and fellowships from prestigious arts foundations such as Creative Capital, Kenneth Rainin Foundation, MAP Fund, National Endowment for the Arts, and Ruth Arts Fellowship. Her current focus is rewilding six acres of land in the Pacific Northwest planting 1,350 native trees with foresters Boots on the Ground. William Talen grew up in small towns throughout Minnesota, South Dakota, and Wisconsin, and came west in the 70s, joining the poetry community in Bolinas, CA before moving to North Beach. Exploring storytelling techniques with solo shows in the Eureka Theater and Intersection, he studied with Spalding Gray and Sidney Lanier. Talen then partnered with Ellen Sebastian, and in 1984 they dreamed of a radical kind of theater, inspired by the stage sets of restaurants and the parties of Anon Salon, eventually lifting “Life on the Water” from a billboard in front of a yuppie apartment complex in Richmond, CA. Gathering with Joe Lambert and Leonard Pitt, LOTW kicked off with six weeks of Gray in the fall of ’86. After seven years, Talen departed for New York, leaving the Solo Mio Festival to Marcia Crosby, Joegh Bullock, and Kate Boyd. In New York and Europe, his character “Reverend Billy” caught a wave of post-religious spiritual hunger, inventing the movement against Consumerism by the time of 9/11. With director and life partner Savitri D, daughter Lena Nightstar, and a revolving troupe of 30 singers, the “Church of Stop Shopping” staged earth services at a series of NYC “art churches” and toured shows on five continents, always returning to justice campaigns in New York. In 2016, Neil Young and Daryl Hannah proposed that Talen preach his “Earthalujah” gospel at the opening of each show, which kicked off a 10-year collaboration, performing in 35 amphitheaters and reaching about 650,000 in Young’s rock audiences. Currently, the Stop Shopping Church has settled in the 500-seat Quaker Meetinghouse in Manhattan, the anti-consumerism of its early days now centered on the Earth’s crisis. Talen’s books include The Earth Wants You from City Lights, and now his fifth book, Earthalujah! , being published in November by Autonomedia Press. Leonard Pitt studied mime in Paris with Etienne Decroux for four years, becoming his assistant and performing in his company. On his return to the U.S., Pitt settled in Berkeley, CA, where he opened a school of physical theater, attracting students from around the world. Pitt’s one-man shows have received critical acclaim. He has performed and taught at theaters and festivals throughout the U.S., Europe, Brazil, New Zealand, and Australia. He was also a member of George Coates Performance Works and traveled widely with the company. In Bali he studied mask theatre and performed extensively with his teacher. In 1986, he co-founded LOTW, where his projects included the “avant-mime” production Not for Real (created with Rinde Eckert), Spleenix , The Art of Face , and performing David Barth’s solo play, Ned . In 1991, Leonard created Eco-Rap, an environmental education program combining ecology and rap music as a way to educate inner city youth about urgent social issues. He has written and published seven books, including three books on Paris and a memoir, and created numerous videos on Paris, all viewable on YouTube ( Leonard Pitt Paris ). He continues to live in Berkeley and create and is currently working on two new books. Joe Lambert is the founder of StoryCenter and the originator of the digital storytelling movement, a participatory media methodology used by 100,000s of people all over the world. The work has taken him and his organization to all 50 U.S. states, and more than 90 countries. Earlier in his career, he served as Executive Director of the People’s Theater Coalition and LOTW, where he executive-produced more than 500 performances, festivals, conferences, and national gatherings. Highlights include the first San Francisco Jazz Tap Festival, collaborations with artists like Guillermo Gomez Peña, the Blue Man Group, Marty Pottenger, and Dana Atchley. During that time, he held leadership roles in national initiatives including the Alliance for Cultural Democracy and the National Performance Network, and served as a panelist and principal consultant for numerous public agencies and private foundations. As an author and curriculum developer, he has written numerous articles. For projToday, based in Santa Fe, NM, he continues this work through StoryHost LLC, teaching workshops, hosting the Elderware podcast, and exploring the intersections of story, aging, and meaning-making. PERFORMERS CIRCUS BY THE BAY : Unique Derique , an internationally acclaimed entertainer, is a cornerstone of the Bay Area circus and performing arts scene. He honed his physical comedy with premier troupes including Circus A La Mode, Make*A*Circus, and the historic Pickle Family Circus. Dedicated to community arts education, Derique has spent nearly three decades as an Artist-in Residence at West Oakland’s Prescott Circus Theater, teaching youth the art and history of Hambone body percussion. His versatile talent has graced international television and stages worldwide, opening for legends like Lou Rawls, Sammy Davis Jr., and The Temptations. Annually, his holiday show Fool La La: Whimsical brings joy to all ages at The Marsh Berkeley. Elise Hing , born and raised in Santa Cruz, CA, discovered her natural flexibility at age 12 and quickly developed a passion for contortion. For the past five years she has performed with Circus Bella doing free shows in the park during the summer and under the big top in the winter for their holiday spectacular. She has also appeared with Flynn Creek Circus and continues to gig all over the bay area. Hing loves to connect and delight audiences through her playful, awe-inspiring shapes and movements but outside of the ring she enjoys being out in nature with friends and pursuing creative projects like sewing. Chloe Somers Walier , known as the “Megawatt Smile,” is an effervescent circus performer with eight years of international touring experience with Les 7 Doigts de la main, performing in Passengers , Duel Reality , and Dear San Francisco . A multidisciplinary performer specializing in hula hoop, trapeze, group acrobatics, and bottle walking – balancing in heels on top of wine bottles – she has performed at three international circus festivals and received the People’s Choice Award from Riga Cirks. With a love for the unexpected and a playful spirit at the heart of her work, she brings a warm, joyful energy to the stage, blending technical skill and theatricality with a little bit of sparkle and a lot of personality. San Francisco Youth Circus (SFYC) performers are part of Circus Center’s pre-professional youth program. 2f4cad4a-cd27-432a-b49d-d2c4e612822a: November 12 – January 16, 2027 Regular Gallery Hours: Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays, 12-5 pm ​(Holiday Schedule: by appointment only from Nov 22-28 and Dec 22 – Jan 2)​​​ Artist’s Reception: Saturday, November 14, 1-4 pm Artist’s Talk: Saturday, January 9th, starting at 2 pm Dana DeKalb’s Statement about No Lifeguard on Duty: Set within a long tradition of narrative art, my figure paintings are riddles, which balance the familiar and nostalgic with the surreal, bringing a psychological charge to seemingly ordinary moments. The enigmatic subjects are situated in improbable dioramas, which glow with the colors of a tinted photograph. With an inner emotion, and a dash of humor, they take on curious tasks and unforeseen events, and are often caught in a moment of decision. At first, they appear engaged in everyday actions; yet on closer inspection, unexpected details reveal that something strange is unfolding. Each scene captures a narrative pause, inviting viewers to unravel the plot and insert their own interpretation to complete the story. No Lifeguard on Duty specifically focuses on the ocean, an iconic environment by turns wildly beautiful, serenely nurturing and dangerously volatile. It’s tidal rhythm of ebb and flow is a symbol of transition and adaptation, serving as an apt metaphor for the fluctuations of life. The figures in the paintings wobble in undersized lifeboats, stilt walk determinedly through high tide, or balance in a human tower on a diving platform. They build sandcastles, play with inflatable toys, and collect specimens from the sea and sky. Like the marooned seafarer Robinson Crusoe, they are portrayed navigating their way through an unpredictable world. In addition to figure paintings, the show features a wall of miniature, detailed panels of undersea zoophytes — an archaic term meaning, literally, “animal-plants” — which transition from lush color to cool monochrome. Mysterious and evocative, they bring to mind alien flora and fauna, while alluding to the bleaching of coral in warming ocean waters.

97fb1247-6163-464b-8682-ab331b91d115: As workers and as parents, we all care deeply about how we must prepare ourselves and our children for fulfilling careers at a time when the changing nature of labor is opaque. In this interactive book talk, co-author Illah Nourbakhsh will share brief remarks regarding our voyage in researching and writing a book about careers, AI and the future of education. We will be joined by two special pioneers who will make brief remarks from the audience: Alan Eustace and Professor Michael Genesereth. Alan Eustace served as senior vice president at Google and has witnessed the digital and AI technology revolutions firsthand. Michael Genesereth is faculty at Stanford University and charted the course of artificial intelligence research as one of its founding scholars. Both Alan and Michael care deeply about the next generation, and the ways in which careers will evolve as AI changes the shape of work. We look forward to a dynamic conversation with the audience. Featuring curated essays from leaders in tech and education, Crunch Time empowers parents, educators, students, and professionals to get informed and access their agency in the AI age. The AI revolution is underway, and none of us are fully prepared. In Crunch Time , education and AI experts Illah Nourbakhsh and Michael Druckman confront one of the central questions of our time: How will artificial intelligence reshape careers, education, and opportunity, and what should we do about it now? Rather than predicting a single future, Crunch Time presents AI as a dynamic, uncertain force that demands informed participation. Originally conceived for educators and parents, the book expands its lens to include students, alumni, mid-career professionals, employers, policymakers, and anyone navigating work and learning in the age of AI. Crunch Time weaves together perspectives from AI inventors, business leaders, educators, technologists, and community leaders, featuring more than forty contributors including AI experts Daniela Rus, Hoda Heidari, Michael Genesereth, Sanjay Sarma, university presidents Nancy Cantor, Lisa Ryerson, Laura Walker, Juan Salgado; business leaders David Siegel, Steve Malony, Dan Draper; visionaries Dame Diane Coyle, William Haseltine, Paul LeBlanc; and leading K to 12 educators. Readers will encounter competing viewpoints, practical guidance, and concrete steps for action. Crunch Time is an invitation to understand, to prepare, and to actively shape a more equitable and human-centered AI future. 3987f64f-0b81-4532-a1f3-a44a9f3cd912: An inspiring guide that reimagines the stages of grief into five healing actions, Reimagining Grief offers light and a new way forward in the midst of darkness. This is the book Kate wishes she'd had, and she wrote it for you. Kate will be joined in conversation by Myra Sacks, the author of award-winning memoir, " Fifty-Seven Fridays: Losing Our Daughter Finding Our Way ," and founder of E-Motion, Inc. There is no way to spin grief. It's hard. It's messy. It's destabilizing. And every single one of us has to go through it. Author and grief coach Kate Doerge knows this too well. Over six years, she lost her father to heart failure and her mother in a car accident five days before Christmas. She also faced the hardest challenge for any parent, losing her sixteen-year-old daughter, Penny, to complications from a rare genetic condition. After Penny's death, Kate knew she had a choice, she could lose herself to a grief so powerful she might not come back from it—or she could find another way through. Reimagining Grief is the result of that search. Drawing from her own experience, the latest research, and conversations with others who have faced devastating loss, Kate offers five actions that can help ground you when you feel out of control, lift you when you're depleted, and help you process the pain of loss. In this book, you'll learn: Why There Isn’t One Right Way to Grieve — and How to Find Your Own Path An Approach to Saying Goodbye That Honors Both You and Your Loved One The 5 Actions Through Grief — and How to Use Them to Heal What Post-Traumatic Growth Really Looks Like How to Find Joy Again Turning Pain into Purpose These actions won’t make grief vanish or disappear; everyone has to go through the difficult path that you are put on after losing someone you loved deeply. However, Reimagining Grief offers some light and healing in the midst of darkness and a different way forward. This is the book Kate wishes she'd had. She wrote it for you. Kate Doerge is a USA TODAY bestselling author, motivational speaker, certified grief coach, and founder of Penny’s Flight Foundation. Through heartfelt storytelling, research-backed insights, and practical strategies, Kate inspires audiences to navigate change, embrace resilience, and lead lives filled with greater purpose and connection. Myra Sack is the author of award-winning memoir, " Fifty-Seven Fridays: Losing Our Daughter Finding Our Way ," and founder of E-Motion, Inc. a nonprofit organization created to support community, movement and ritual to enhance coping and resilience. Myra's life changed when her older daughter, Havi, died in January 2021. Blending Myra's lived experience and knowledge as a certified Compassionate Bereavement Care provider with her lifelong identity as an athlete and career in social impact, E-Motion evolved out of a new way of living with the most difficult reality. Myra holds an MBA in Social Impact from Boston University, and graduated with a B.A. cum laude from Dartmouth College, where she captained the women's soccer team and earned All-America honors. Myra serves on the Board of the Courageous Parents Network. adf26ce2-c44b-4c7a-a37e-010d2aa33aa4: Matt shares his dramatic tale of gentlemen-explorers of the 1930s racing to find and harvest a poisonous Amazon vine. Join us at Mrs. Dalloway's Bookstore on Thursday, November 12 at 7:00 PM when Matt O'Hara comes to the store to present his new book The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon . Matt will be joined by Rebecca Herman for the conversation and will sign copies of his book after the presentation. In the fall of 1938, a young, frail American explorer set off down a river in the western Amazon in search of curare, a poison he thought might save his life. Richard Gill had learned that local tribes used curare-laced blow darts to kill animals, but it was also potentially a cure for many ailments, including his own. He also thought he could make a fortune by connecting the knowledge of two worlds. Obsessed with curare, he raced to make deals with Indigenous poison masters in the Amazon and pharmaceutical companies back home, even as his Russian-born rival Boris Krukoff sought to do the same. In The Flying Death , the historian Matt O'Hara asks who and what we are willing to sacrifice in the name of discovery and profit. O'Hara brings to life Gill's epic quest, a stranger-than-fiction true story that moves from unexplored territory in the Amazon to rogue medical trials and cutthroat corporate boardrooms in the United States. Navigating treacherous terrain and politics, Gill and Krukoff successfully created a veritable curare–industrial complex, as the plant became a key element in shock therapy, transformed surgery in the United States and across the globe, and eventually led to a Nobel Prize. The Flying Death offers a thrilling ride across Indigenous knowledge, scientific exploration, and exploitation, unearthing a story of discovery that poses searching questions about the price of progress, who pays it, and who gets credit. MATT O'HARA is a professor of history at the University of California, Santa Cruz. He is the award-winning author of many journal articles and two books, The History of the Future in Colonial Mexico and A Flock Divided: Race, Religion, and Politics in Mexico, 1749–1857. REBECCA HERMAN is Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley, where she teaches about environmental politics, US-Latin American relations, and modern Latin America. She is the author of Cooperating with the Colossus: A Social and Political History of US Military Bases in World War II Latin America and is currently at work on a book about anti-extractivism in Antarctica. Her first novel, The Outposters , will be published next summer by Cardinal.

eb700ee2-4f20-4efc-ac01-8755d2bde6b2: Join us on Thursday, November 12 at 7pm for Weird Science, Strange Beliefs, and the Impossible, an evening with authors Scott Lambridis, Martha Conway, and Yance Wyatt at 9th Ave! Free to Attend, Please RSVP Or Watch on YouTube Live/Link Available Soon About the Event Weird Science, Strange Beliefs, and the Impossible In celebration of the release of their new books, three novelists discuss the pleasures and perils of making the impossible believable. From alternate histories and afterlives to strange science, mythology, and dark humor, Scott Lambridis (St. Ulphia’s Dead), Martha Conway (We Meet Apart), and Yance Wyatt (The Watersmith) explore how fiction destabilizes what we think we know—and what becomes possible when writers allow uncertainty to remain unresolved—in a conversation moderated by writer and critic Olga Zilberbourg. The authors will share brief passages from their new work that speak to the evening’s theme, then dig into genre, research, belief, and the craft of making an impossible premise reveal something emotionally true. About the Authors Martha Conway is the author of several award-winning novels including The Underground River, which was a New York Times Book Editor’ s Choice and published in seven languages. Her short fiction has appeared in The Iowa Review, The Missouri Review, Folio, and other journals. Martha was awarded a California Arts Council Fellowship for Creative Writing, and she teaches creative writing for Stanford University’ s Continuing Studies. She lives with her family in San Francisco. Born and raised in New York, Scott Lambridis earned a degree in neurobiology from the University of Virginia. He’ s toured the Midwest with a progressive rock band, founded an indie press and performance series, earned an MFA from San Francisco State University, tended a 40-acre olive farm, and read a book from every country of the world. He wrote St. Ulphia’ s Dead during his daughter’ s naps during a year in France, and finally settled with his wife and child in Bellingham, Washington, “ the city of subdued excitement.” This is his first novel. Yance Wyatt is from Nashville, Tennessee, or thereabouts. He studied fiction at the University of Southern California, where he now teaches writing. His stories have appeared in dozens of nationally circulated literary journals and received multiple Pushcart Prize nominations. He lives with his wife and son in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains. The Watersmith is his first novel.
fe38d002-6cd7-47d8-8546-6ffcc5fa6351: Books Inc. Palo Alto welcomes local author Mike Trigg back to the store to celebrate his new novel Outage! Mike will be in conversation with fellow local author Kathy Oneto. Join us to hear these authors discuss their writing process, get a reading from Outage, and participate in an audience Q&A. About Outage: For fans of Laura Dave's The Last Thing He Told Me and William R. Forstchen's One Second After comes a riveting thriller about an internet blackout that leads one woman into a web of lies and conspiracies and her pursuit for answers. Rachel Farrell is working from home in suburban Virginia when the internet goes out. Juggling clients, two restless teenagers, and dinner logistics with her husband, Caleb, a DC lobbyist, she assumes it’s just a routine inconvenience. Then she finds his note , warning they are in danger and not to trust anyone . When FBI agents show up looking for Caleb, Rachel realizes something far more sinister is underway: a nationwide internet and phone outage, and Caleb’s biggest client—a powerful Chinese semiconductor company—is at the center of suspicion. As the night wears on with no word from Caleb, Rachel’s unease shifts into something darker. The man she has been married to for two decades may not be who she thought he was. Fearing for their safety, Rachel and her children embark on a harrowing cross-country journey to find Caleb and hear his explanation. But the more she learns, the more she suspects he may be in on the plot. Following the clues to a remote compound in South Dakota, Rachel begins to piece together the truth about her husband, his business dealings, and a conspiracy that reaches far beyond anything she ever imagined. In the end, Rachel has no choice but to uncover the real culprit behind the outage before it costs her everything. Mike Trigg grew up in Wisconsin and now lives in the San Francisco Bay Area with his wife and two sons. He earned a BA from Northwestern University and an MBA from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to becoming an author, he worked in the Silicon Valley technology industry for over twenty years. His first novel, Bit Flip , was released in August 2022 to critical acclaim, lauded as a “twisty, acerbic corporate thriller” by the San Francisco Chronicle , “exceptionally well-written” by IndieReader, and “an engrossing novel” by Foreword. Trigg’s second novel, Burner , was released in April 2024 and praised as a “searing, all-too-believable novel” by BookLife Reviews and “a cautionary tale for the digital age” by IndieReader. Trigg’s work has been featured in Publisher’s Weekly , Kirkus , and Literary Hub . He has been a contributor to TechCrunch , Entrepreneur , and Fast Company , and regularly posts on his author site, www.miketrigg.com . Kathy Oneto is an executive and life-work coach, speaker, and facilitator who is committed to helping people thrive on their terms, both in life and in work. She is also a strategy executive who bridges her two worlds by applying strategic approaches to life and work decisions and practices. Kathy started asking questions at a young age about success, ambition, and navigating life and work and has used her work and career as a touchstone to guide decisions at different stages in her life. As she reflected on her adult life and career, she found that she had been intuitively living and working according to the Sustainable Ambition Method. Today, she works with clients and company employees in applying the method and helping them find personal motivation in their work and goals, architect their next life and work arcs, and manage their effort for more resilience and sustainability. As a strategist, Kathy has had a twenty-five-year career working across business, branding, innovation, and talent. In her work today, she helps organizations illuminate their most compelling value and build strategic road maps to guide sustainable action. Proud of her public education, Kathy has a BS in commerce from the University of Virginia and received her MBA from the University of California, Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. Her writing has appeared in Fast Company , Brandingmag , and MediaPost . She’s been a guest lecturer at the business schools at Berkeley, the University of San Francisco, Duke University, and the University of Colorado. Kathy lives in San Francisco with her husband and the fog. As a former triathlete and marathon runner, she’s happiest building up her resilience and sustainability outdoors, where you can often find her running in Golden Gate Park, walking the streets of her city or one she’s traveled to, or enjoying the experience of reading with the sun on her face. You can connect with her at SustainableAmbition.com .
06b8ff04-ab15-4e66-a82c-89c13ed77627: Contemporary saxophonist, author, and music producer Jackiem Joyner is set to release his 7th album, Touch, worldwide this fall, 2019. After more than 12 years as a recording artist, Jackiem continues to stand out with electrifying live performances and brilliant music productions. As a performer, he has toured over 30 countries and performed with the likes of the late George Duke, Marcus Miller, Keiko Matsui, Donnie McClurkin, Angela Bofill, Najee, Kirk Whalum, Peter White, and many, many more. Joyner’s radio success is widely known within the industry. Joyner has two number-one hit songs, five top 10 Billboard singles, and a number-one debut album under his belt. In addition, he published the highly acclaimed science fiction novel Zarya , which received high praise and a five-star rating on Amazon. “This album is about romance,” Joyner explains of Touch . “I wanted to give everyone something hip, smooth, and sexy at the same time.” The record has an urban feel, laced with the hottest downtempo vibes. The album shares similar textures to the music of artists Tank and Trey Songz. Joyner’s soprano sax leads the charge through most of the album. “My approach to performing on this record was to be melodic and dynamic with my horn”. Peter White joins Jackiem on the first single, “Last Dance”. The combination of soprano sax and nylon guitar pulls you in with its romantic and catchy melody. Najee serves up the flute on a dreamy urban song called “Fairytales”. The unique mix of flute and soprano sax on this vibey tune forms one of Joyner’s best performances and productions. The song was written together with Tim Bailey, aka Twizzboy. Born to a Vietnam War veteran father and a dedicated mother in Norfolk, VA, growing up wasn’t easy for Jackiem. He set his sights high from a young age; he always dreamed of being a performing artist, as unlikely as it was, given his humble upbringing. Even as a child, he loved the attention he received from his family when he danced to Michael Jackson songs. Now, Jackiem is proud to stand front and center on the main stage most weekends around the country. A quick glance at Joyner’s track record makes it clear that he continues to beat the odds in a tough and competitive music industry. “I love what I do, and I have passion”, Jackiem says. “I don’t care how hard things get, it’ll never stop me from doing what I love: playing the sax, writing music and stories, and performing live.” His love of writing novels came as a surprise to many of his fans. “I’m very excited to release my second novel soon after my album release,” Joyner says. “Writing stories is now a big part of my creative journey.” The first single from Joyner’s last album, Main Street Beat (2017), was named for his daughter, Trinity. Joyner’s adoration for his little girl is clearly expressed through the live, pop-influenced song, driven by Steve Oliver’s guitar. The song was an instant hit. Reaching no. 2 on the Billboard. We’re all dying to see if she follows in dad’s footsteps with her own stage career someday! With the creation of his company, JOYNER MEDIA COMPANY L.L.C., Joyner hopes to inspire other creators to follow their dreams and realize their true potential in art and multimedia. When Jackiem is not touring the world, he spends time giving lectures to students across the country. He also enjoys talking to band classes, helping them with practice, and offering insight on how to pursue a career in the performing arts. Currently, Joyner is on a US tour in support of his new album, Touch . He will be touring Los Angeles, CA – Washington, DC – Hampton, VA – Melbourne, FL – Detroit, MI – Chicago, IL – Charleston, SC – Houston, TX – Rehoboth Beach, DE – Mazlatan, Mexico – Syracuse, NY – Tampa, FL – Atlanta, GA, and many more cities.

Between them, 2022 NEA Jazz Master Stanley Clarke and 1998 NEA Jazz Master Ron Carter have defined and redefined the bass’s role in modern jazz, from the hard bop innovations of the early 1960s to the jazz-fusion revolution of the 1970s and 1980s. The four-time GRAMMY winning Clarke achieved worldwide fame as a pioneer of jazz fusion with Chick Corea and Return to Forever, and his subsequent career as a bandleader. The Philadelphia native has recorded 24 albums as a leader, leading a procession of masterful bands, and collaborating with George Duke, McCoy Tyner, Dexter Gordon, Freddie Hubbard, Al Di Meola, Paul McCartney, Keith Richards, Stewart Copeland, and dozens more. Ron Carter is, quite simply, the face of jazz bass. A towering figure, he was already a creative force on the roiling early ‘60s scene when he joined Miles Davis in 1962, the first piece of what became the trumpeter’s second great quintet. With more than 2,300 albums to his credit, including over 60 as a leader, "The Maestro” holds the Guinness World Record as jazz’s most recorded bassist. Clarke and Carter collaborated in a trio with guitarist Russell Malone as part of the recent PBS documentary on Carter’s life, Ron Carter: Finding the Right Notes. aa6bc4fb-c57f-4399-af5d-aec0889f504b: (Please do not bring infants to the show) Born into a radical theater company, Joyful Raven was tasked from the tender age of 5 with the daunting mission to save the world from impending doom… using theater. Forced into animal-print unitards and political positions long before she was a consenting adult, she never had a fighting chance at anything resembling a normal life. You think your parents were embarrassing? Did you have to sing about salmon sex on stage, in a unitard, at 12 years old… WITH your parents? I didn’t think so. In an attempt to heal her hippie trauma, she runs away from home to seek solace in the arms of a spiritual teacher… and accidentally finds herself in the yoga-to-fascism pipeline. Can she save herself? Can she save the world… using theater?! Or does she have to choose? Blending standup, drag, storytelling, & clown, Raven takes audiences on a dystopian and hilarious romp through the looking glass. Joyful Raven is an award-winning actor, director, and “story midwife” known for her powerful and thought-provoking solo shows, where she tackles thorny social issues with humor, heart, and nuance. Born into an iconic political theater family, she has been devising original work for over 20 years. Joyful holds an MFA in Dramatic Art from the University of California, Davis, and teaches solo performance and storytelling at Berkeley Rep School of Theatre, The Marsh, and her own studio in Berkeley. Dara Kosberg is a storyteller, comedian, and writer. She debuted her solo storytelling show “Homecoming” to sold-out shows in NYC, LA, Atlanta and Chicago. She’s a Moth StorySlam winner and has performed at San Francisco’s Punch Line Comedy Club and Brooklyn’s Union Hall. As part of the Reimagine End of Life arts festival in SF and NYC, she’s produced and performed in comedy shows about grief and loss that demonstrate the healing power of humor. Piece Description – Homecoming Dara’s 15 minute piece is an excerpt of “Homecoming”, her solo show that was recently nominated for the Comedic Theatre Award and StageCrafts’ Freeway Circuit Award at the 2026 Hollywood Fringe Festival. A dark comedy, “Homecoming” begins when Dara is studying art in Australia when she gets that call— her mom is dying, and she has to come home. Suddenly, their already difficult mother/daughter relationship becomes a lot more complicated. How do you make amends with a dead mom? What follows is a winding journey through the awkward, painful, unexpectedly hilarious process of finding yourself again after loss. Directed by David Ford, Artist-in- Residence at The Marsh.
