540d7871-e687-4aab-aa9f-d474db637e81: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: School Fair School Fair (Findlay Buchanan, Semisi Ma’ia’i, Hamish Morgan, De Stevens and Rose Pickernell) make music embedded in the human experience. It’s a product of the band’s native New Zealand, a place that remains intimate and remote, where emotion is magnified over both distance and familiarity. The five band members began the project renting out a factory-sized, sub-zero degree Celsius room normally operated by construction workers in the industrial area of Ōtepoti, Dunedin, New Zealand in 2021, recording music on the 4-track tape recorder that would become debut Gorse on a Hill . The album remained the only trace of the band online for a few years, an artifact for those who know where to look. School Fair’s music has this sense of self-discovery when you find it, a sound that feels both recognizable and like the vacant expanse of a country whirring by on a train. Still with little to no self-promotion, the appearance of sophomore effort Bird the Kid online in early 2025 was a new portal to their world of melodic and intricate indie music that retains a kind of atmospheric beauty. Unexpected Violence (Mutual, 2026) is the first record made between geographical places, with the band now split in between London and New Zealand. You can hear this fragmented approach in the patchwork quality and inherent connective tissue of the album. Recorded initially in a studio in East London, it was the first time the band brought in an outside engineer (Syd Kemp?), as opposed to the band’s prior live recordings, where the tendency was to “feed back off each other in quite a messy abstract and complicated way that works for us but isn’t typically structured.” The band then took these recordings and evolved them back home in Dunedin, with the addition of vocals on some tracks by Pickernell adding to the cohesive energy and collective, dialed-in synergy of the quintet. School Fair is built upon the many eclectic mediums from which the band members individually create: time spent repairing old machines, making short films, metalworking and jewelry-making, writing and engineering. All these counterparts bring a kind of industrial electricity to the music where each part feels necessary and agile, as well as perfectly in conjunction. It’s these points beneath the surface where the songs really bloom. The moody transference of guitar lick to guttural vocal and back again, where melody conjoins with surprising inflection and sharp-hued ambiance, littered with both poetic spoken-word and a self-referentiality of clues and repetition that rewards close listening yet remains accessible and immediate. Transportive lyrics shine with the lore and mythology of a world that is both deeply specific and transcendent in its curiosity toward the surrounding environment. Unexpected Violence is filled with resounding descriptors: from “cat runs blind in the smoke / birds slap their wings away / trees thrash and crash / each lonely in their chosen way” (the meandering “Angelika”) or the consequently spellbinding phrasing of “come out to your dead animal river gushing hard / come out to your heart split open and lit up with stars” of “In Boredom You Shoot Your Gun”. It’s a starkly poetic snapshot into the band’s own universe and a showcase in the thoroughfare of language, where the specificity of one person’s memory counteracts with a landscape that blurs and unravels with the passage of time. Unexpected Violence a record that could only be made in a place like New Zealand, yet its vantage point expands far beyond to the vast unwieldiness of human sentiment. “There’s a sense of remoteness to the record, both emotionally but also in the sense of place, broken farms, cast iron beaches, blank midday fires, lost friends.” Or as the band recites in the austere glimmer of “Spirally Staircase Memory”: “memories are just stories that can’t be found.” But School Fair reaches some sort of access point, a way for them to live on. The name Unexpected Violence was born out of Buchanan and Ma’ia’i coming across the genre title in a bookstore in Berlin, and is a fitting discernment of the heartbreak that often comes with the realities of existence. In album highlight “Gussied Up,” the band intones: “I never never never ever / wanna hear you / see you, feel you or touch you.” It’s a harsh statement that feels swept up in the parallel admission that these are relationships you may never fully escape; they have left their mark. We still pass the places they inhabit, and feel the uncanny emptiness even after moving on. It’s fitting that the record ends on a similar contradiction. Just discernable above spirals of drummed up, ambient noise: “I miss you now you’re gone.” For all things can be true at once. This practice strengthens the immune system, supports the body’s natural capacity to heal, and cultivates mental clarity and emotional steadiness. Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. Her work invites students to explore the foundations of Qigong and Tai Chi as embodied, healing practices that cultivate awareness, vitality, and resilience.

af2c849b-ac12-425c-aa43-e3f0fb1b9d34: “ To Stay, To Stay, To Stay is about the great contradiction of love, that it brings both great bafflement and great clarity, and somehow, ultimately, isn’t a contradiction. So much hard-earned daily wisdom here. I needed this book. You probably do too.”—Peter Orner, author of The Gossip Columnist’s Daughter Devon will be joined in conversation by Daniel Gumbiner, the author of Fire in the Canyon. An ensemble cast collides and crosses paths in their small corner of the Midwest where no one is a stranger: the baker, the realtor, the poet, the gardener, the frustrated artist. In Devon Halliday’s transcendent debut novel, secrets turn contagious, impulses transform into resolutions, and no one is certain whether they will remain in the confines of their Appalachian college town or step out into the unknown. Surrounded by hills, buried in green, Eden is a forgotten town full of ordinary lives. But over the course of a humid summer week, seven of these ordinary lives reach their boiling point, as the existential questions of each begin to urgently entwine. Underneath the threat of marital infidelity, financial ruin, and life-changing illness is always the same question: To stay, or to go? If you choose to stay, is it ever a permanent choice? Can you be sure you’ll choose it again tomorrow? A mosaic portrait of love and its close substitutes, the novel suggests, fearfully, that even our best decisions might be fragile, arbitrary, and impermanent. “This brims with insights into the human condition.”— Publishers Weekly “A heartfelt debut … Halliday offers varied, honest looks at the intimate struggles that accompany life’s unexpected turning points.”— Booklist “Devon Halliday has such a mastery of language and storytelling artistry that it’s hard to believe To Stay, To Stay, To Stay is her debut. This novel, a wry and incisive exploration of how people behave (and misbehave) at the critical inflection points in their lives, is a marvel.”—Marisa Silver, author of At Last “In this enchanting tale of small-town love, artisanal bread, and sketchy real estate, Devon Halliday explores the webs that connect us and the mysterious forces that break those webs apart. Everything and everyone in this wonderful novel is rendered with precision, wit, and uncompromising humanity.”—David Haynes, author of Martha’s Daughter “With rare emotional precision and a fierce, glowing heart, Devon Halliday investigates the stories people tell themselves about love and the combustible, constant anxieties that sustain those stories. This marvelous debut novel wisely asks an urgent, contemporary question: What’s braver? Blowing up your life? Or simply living it, however it unfolds?”—Dean Bakopoulos, author of Summerlong “What a delightful debut novel by Devon Halliday—its pages full of sun and shadow, love and gravity. To Stay, To Stay, To Stay handles its cast of characters with deftness and grace, showing us the many facets of people in a small town as they connect and disconnect from one another.”—Alix Ohlin, author of Dual Citizens “A preternaturally wise and wickedly ambitious debut. Halliday’s small town and big cast of characters cast a spell under which I would happily have stayed, stayed, stayed. Alas, the ending is perfection, too.”—Anna Solomon, author of The Book of V Devon Halliday is a Pushcart Prize winner and a Rona Jaffe Foundation Graduate Fellow. Her writing appears in Ploughshares , One Story , the Los Angeles Review of Books , and Lit Hub , among other journals. Her debut novel To Stay, To Stay, To Stay has been longlisted for the Center for Fiction First Novel Prize. Daniel Gumbiner’s first novel, The Boatbuilder (2018), was a nominee for the National Book Award and a finalist for the California Book Award. His second book, Fire in the Canyon (2023), was a finalist for the California Book Award and a New Yorker Best Book of the Year. He is the Editor of The Believer and lives in San Francisco. As a high schooler, he worked as a barista at the Book Passage Cafe in Corte Madera. 2dbb82e5-4a18-4e25-ad9b-d5da2b94903c: Kyle Connaughton began his culinary career in L.A. with an apprenticeship at one of the oldest Japanese restaurants in the city and continued training in both pastry and savory at Spago Beverly Hills, The Dining Room at Ritz Carlton, Lucques, Hama Sushi, and A.O.C. This was followed by several years cooking in Japan for the famed chef Michel Bras and in numerous traditional Japanese cuisine restaurants. In 2006, Kyle joined Heston Blumenthal to become the Head Chef of Research and Development for the Fat Duck Experimental Kitchen. He is a contributor to the “Modernist Cuisine” series, a co-developer of the Culinary Science Bachelors Degree program for the CIA, and co-author of the book Donabe – Classic and Modern Japanese Clay Pot Cooking. In 2014 Kyle co-founded the culinary development firm Pilot R+D with Dan Felder, Dr. Ali Bouzari, & Dana Peck. Katina Connaughton and her husband Kyle have been together since they met at 15. Katina began her first foray into farming while living in a rural agricultural community in Hokkaido, Japan. She continued culinary gardening on a Victorian estate property in England before moving to Sonoma to complete her coursework in Sustainable Agriculture and Horticulture. Katina was greenhouse manager for the Ag Program and Santa Rosa Junior College and has farmed at Davis Family Winery and The Barlow. Katina heads up SingleThread Farm at Dry Creek 24 acre property, greenhouses, heirloom orchards and bee hives well as the foraging program and floral design department SingleThread — At Single Thread, each meal tells the story of the day. Each menu, and every dish on it, is designed to reflect that specific moment in time and to showcase the ingredients grown on the SingleThread farm. But the approach taken by Kyle and Katina Connaughton (SingleThread’s chef and farmer co-founders) does not end with a simple commitment to seasonality and locality. Instead, it involves a nuanced, considered approach that balances this celebration of local ingredients with a holistic view of what constitutes good food systems—including the need to support artisans, preserve the expertise developed by generations of specialists, and develop climate-resilient approaches to farming and other forms of food production. SingleThread offers a deep dive into what truly seasonal cooking looks like and into the mindful approach Kyle and Katina take to every aspect of their work, from their warm hospitality to the meticulous design philosophy behind the restaurant and inn. With stunning photography and intricate illustrations, the book offers a tour of the farm and restaurant while also delving into the team’s unique agricultural methods, the techniques and recipes used in the SingleThread kitchen, the way the farm and kitchen teams coordinate on a daily basis, their philosophy of hospitality, the importance of their relationships with other producers and artisans—and the unique love story that started with two teenagers at a punk show and grew into the partnership that made all of this possible in the first place.

88769b32-7f02-43b1-9b35-d2c77c523604: Sarang Byrne was born and raised in Miami, Florida, where she was encouraged from a young age to pursue art. After attending New World School of the Arts High School, she earned her BFA in Illustration Design from ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, California. Byrne creates expressive watercolor paintings inspired by plants and flowers, balancing recognizable forms with abstraction, gestural brushwork, and bold color. Her process embraces the unpredictability of watercolor, allowing each painting to unfold organically through movement, experimentation, and intuition. She now lives and works in San Francisco’s Outer Sunset neighborhood. About the show: A flower brought home, a plant tended over time, photos taken during my travels— each offers a starting point for these abstract floral paintings. I aim to transform botanical forms into something entirely my own. Working intuitively with watercolor, I allow the paint to move and interact in unexpected ways, following the work wherever it leads. The result exists somewhere between observation and abstraction, where the original subject may emerge or dissolve into color and form. As I continue to understand and experiment with my art practice, I find myself wanting to put the work out into the world as a way of understanding it better. Showing the work publicly is part of the process for me — a chance to step outside of the studio, look at what I’ve made, and see what it has to say back. Please feel free to reach out to me if you have any questions or comments – sarang@sarangbyrne.com Thank you for being here and taking the time to view my work, I truly appreciate it! Sarang

d674c0ad-a876-4466-b9e2-754313a3cfaf: Neil Young Celebration Neil Young Tribute from local musicians plus a screening of Rust Never Sleeps To celebrate the 81st birthday of one of our all-time favorites, a group of local musicians are coming together to honor the iconic work of Neil Young. The set will be followed by a screening of his iconic San-Francisco-set concert film Rust Never Sleeps . Singer/songwriter Neil Young is sometimes visionary, sometimes flaky, sometimes both at once, but he has never been boring. Indeed, Neil Young has weathered runs of critical and popular ambivalence only to be vindicated by being periodically "rediscovered" by young musicians and fans. He has maintained a large following since the early '70s with music in three basic styles — solo acoustic ballads, sweet country rock, and lumbering garage rock (with some experimental music side trips), all topped by his high voice — and he veers from one to another in unpredictable phases. His subject matter also shifts from personal confessions to allusive stories to bouncy throwaways. A dedicated primitivist, Young is constantly proving that simplicity is not always simple. Rust Never Sleeps is a concert film shot on Neil Young's 1978 U.S. tour, filmed at the Cow Palace in San Francisco. Divided into two segments, acoustic and electric, the film is Young at his best, shown just why the grunge generation holds him in such high esteem, and that not all 60's heroes were burnt out by the mid-70's. Teaching everything from self-creation to stopping violence; from vegetarianism to transcendental meditation, from the establishment of Hip Hop Appreciation Week (every third week in May), to establishing Hip Hop as an international culture at the United Nations (2001), KRS-One has single-handedly held the history and original arts of Hip Hop together now for over two decades. 6eb8074a-6a6d-429c-b661-9feee0319396: When asked to describe himself, Whitmer Thomas—comic, musician, skateboarder, infamous Blink182 stan—will tell you, “I’m always gonna be the one whose mom called him ‘the Golden One,’ right before she died.” This is where his debut HBO comedy special, The Golden One, finds Whitmer: age thirty, investigating this sense (curse?) of destiny-as-identity. It’s been thirteen years since he left Alabama for LA, becoming a linchpin for LA’s young, independent comedy scene with Power Violence, the monthly show he hosted with friends. But he became haunted by the question: had he already peaked, just like his mom, singer in a local band with big ambitions that never made it out of the Flora-Bama Lounge in Gulf Shores? Rather than shy away from all that messy self-mythology, Whitmer tapped the source of it all through writing this one-man show featuring his own original music. Songs from The Golden One, a companion album of songs from the special, features Whitmer’s darkwave bangers, synthesizing relatable-content: millennial anxieties, therapy-speak jokes, and the annals of his own childhood tragedies. Songs from The Golden One feature ten cuts of borderline-John Maus cosplay with spasms of pop-punk absurdity. Thomas uses the gothy, nasal vocal drone as a tool of comic detachment to cover thr funny-’cause-its-true territory of awkward sex, crippling insecurity, the shame of ambition, and the long tail of abandonment traumas. Each song is a capsule of initial therapy breakthroughs: those realization-zingers where suddenly it all makes sense, how each fucked variable from then makes up the weird shit of now. When you see it all for what it is, it looks like some sick, clever joke from the universe, driving you desperate to revise the comedy so that if you have to be reality’s punchline, at least you can write the jokes. Original tracks from the special include the shimmering, synthy euphoria of “Eat You Out,” a glorious admission to performance anxiety and the ol’ magician’s cloak of cunnilingus move. There’s “The Codependent Enabler,” a whole jungle gym of toxic relationship rationale where “I can only get it up if you are down,” and the sadboy sobriety anthem “Partied to Death,” about when you’re young in LA and you have to tell people that you’re not *Cali sober for wellness*, but because your mom actually died from addiction, so. At first pass, Whitmer’s special and album make a relevant, hilarious articulation of one tragic childhood, of the messiness of masculinity, of the timeless qualms of being broke with a dream in Los Angeles, and the humiliation inherent in having “a dream” at all. But in flashes of unexpected weirdo wisdom, Whitmer weaves a deeper story of a person finding reconciliation and forgiveness alongside finding his own self and voice. He faces his darkness with darkwave, writing the story of his objectively insane youth through a Venn diagram of cool guy music, goofy dude jokes, and sensitive boy reflections that hit in a way that feels bigger than the sum of its parts. Whitmer will say that he made The Golden One out of desperation, but there’s something about the show feels a lot more, instead, like destiny.

Questions or comments? Please contact us at membership@museumca.org or 510-318-8520. On View at AAM Ha Chong-Hyun: Retrospective For over six decades, pioneering artist Ha Chong-Hyun (b. 1935) has explored what painting becomes when freed from all existing conventions. Ha’s work prizes the interaction of his materials: using pressure, gravity, and tools ranging from torches to everyday utensils, he transforms the surfaces of canvases up to eight feet tall into a treasure trove of texture and physicality. His first museum exhibition in North America, Ha Chong-Hyun: Retrospective offers an unprecedented look at the creative evolution of one of Korea’s most influential contemporary artists. Garuda in Bali From his birth as a precious egg to his decision to serve as the vehicle of the Hindu god Vishnu, the divine adventures of Garuda come to life in this evocative exhibition. Part-bird, part-man, and the epitome of loyalty and courage, Garuda holds profound significance not only as a fierce warrior, but as the archetype of a deeply devoted son. Featuring wooden sculptures and traditional paintings from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the exhibition traces Garuda’s legendary exploits, capturing both the artistic mastery of Balinese creators and the enduring spiritual resonance of a protector deity who remains central to Indonesian culture today. Art from Contemporary Cambodia Beyond the ancient temples of Angkor lies a deeply compelling contemporary art scene. This exhibition spotlights works by Sopheap Pich and Leang Seckon, two of Cambodia’s most internationally prominent artists. Born in the 1970s, both lived through the Khmer Rouge genocide and emerged in the early 2000s as key figures in the country’s artistic revival. While their styles differ greatly, both artists transform everyday materials from Cambodia in distinctive ways. Seckon, using photographs, paint, and recycled textiles, builds collages that contemplate the traumas of the past and the complexities of the present. Pich uses natural materials and discarded objects to craft tactile, abstract sculptures, which he sees as distillations of his remembrances and emotions. Kim Minwook: On Carving, Bending, and Binding Wood Kim Minwook (b. 1978, South Korea) works with wood shaped by weather, time, and nature. Attentive to his raw material, Kim responds to the grain, tension, and movement already present, and allows cracks, knots, or scars to inform the work, thus carrying forth the life of the tree into sculpture. “The wood itself is an active presence,” says Assistant Curator of Korean Art Yoon-Jee Choi, “not simply an object shaped by the artist, but a collaborator.” Kim’s adventurous approach to his medium is on full display in his first solo museum exhibition, On Carving, Bending, and Binding Wood. A self-taught craftsman, Kim discovered his passion for woodturning in 2013 and earned swift recognition, receiving the 2019 Lexus Creative Masters Award in Seoul, and shortlisted for the 2022 Loewe Foundation Craft Prize. Kim continues to reimagine contemporary craft through a practice grounded in listening to material, time, and the quiet narratives held within wood. Through movement, play, somatic awareness, and guided conversations, we'll explore what happens when we let ourselves show up more fully and meet one another more deeply. Rather than trying to “get connection right,” we’ll explore what naturally allows connection to emerge—through presence, play, movement, and authentic conversation. " — PITCHFORK Like Devendra Banhart’s music and visual art, his poetry appears at the convergence of humor and sorrow, tragedy and joy. With Four Nose Jobs A Day , Banhart’s second collection, the poet explores matters of the heart and soul through an absurdist lens both sly and compassionate. As the opening lines of the collection alert us, Banhart loves “a Love Poem/One that reads/Like Blackberries/On a wooden cup”. With iconoclastic verve, Banhart builds small, often silly paths of poetic language that lead to meaningful conclusions: “Poetry is when/the dead end/Starts to go somewhere” Like professional musicians constantly on tour, Banhart reminds us that we, the readers, have countless places to visit both in the world around us, and inside ourselves—whether these places resonate and register is up to us, not the places. The poems of Four Nose Jobs A Day break the surface of reality, small bubbles of insight. Sometimes there is laughter in the face of absurdity; consolation for grief or despair; and sometimes there is simply gratitude. “What an Honor,” the poet reminds us, “To have emotions/Any of them.” **** Devendra Banhart is a Venezuelan-American singer-songwriter and visual artist. His drawings have been exhibited, among others, at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Centre for Fine Arts in Brussels, and Los Angeles’ Museum of Contemporary Art. He has released over ten albums and has performed at venues such as Carnegie Hall, Bonnaroo, and Coachella. This is one of many books he has published. He lives in Los Angeles. Aggregate Vision November 5 – January 9, 2027 Regular Gallery Hours: Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays, 12-5 pm ​(Holiday Schedule: by appointment only from Nov 22-28 and Dec 22 – Jan 2)​​​ Transmission Gallery is pleased to present Aggregate Vision, a solo exhibition of recent work by Tiffany Schmierer in the Small Space of the gallery, at the top of the stairs. Schmierer’s ceramic sculptures bring together an intricate vocabulary of color, pattern, texture, and form. Constructed from interlocking shapes and multi-planar facets, the works balance geometric structure with organic movement. Each element has its own surface, pattern, and character, yet contributes to a larger composition of surprising connections and visual complexity anchored by repeated motifs. Through multiple glaze firings, Schmierer builds richly layered surfaces, combining varied colors, graphic patterns, and tactile details. Curves, angles, ridges, and open spaces intersect and overlap, creating a sense of movement and depth. As the eye travels across the work, individual forms shift in relation to one another, revealing new patterns and spatial relationships. The interplay of structure, color, and surface gives the work an animated quality, while the complexity of their construction holds the parts together as a cohesive whole.
02f70276-aa6a-4db6-aefc-b016f894b1f8: Please join us for a reading by LeeAnn Pickrell from her new book, Tsunami . This event is organized by the Left Coast Writers and hosted by Book Passage. This story explores the tsunami through a lens of separation, reunion, and the psychic shifts of such an experience. It is a moving account of coming home, letting go of outdated faith, and discovering the connections forged through the stories we tell. On the morning of December 26, 2004, an undersea earthquake struck off the coast of Sumatra in the Indian Ocean. The resulting tsunami killed an estimated 230,000 people across fourteen countries, from Indonesia to Sri Lanka to Thailand to the Maldives to India and all the way to East Africa. Everyone who was there and survived has a story of where they were when the tsunami hit. But there are too many stories that will never be told. This is one woman's story of her experience of that day and its aftermath.LeeAnn Pickrell was in Rai Leh, Thailand, just off the beach drinking coffee that morning when the ocean went away. Everyone ran to the top of the beach to see a wall of white approaching the shore, at first slowly and then picking up speed as boats overturned and they realized the wave wasn't going to stop. It's the story of the tsunami in a particular place, of not understanding what was happening, of separation and reunion. It's also a story of coming home, of not being hurt physically but the psychic shifts of such an experience. It's about letting go of old ideas of faith that no longer make sense and opening to the connections we have to each other through the stories we tell. LeeAnn Pickrell is the author of Tsunami (Unsolicited Press, 2026). Her debut collection, Gathering the Pieces of Days , was published in 2025 by Unsolicited Press. She is also the author of the chapbook Punctuated , published by Bottlecap Press in 2024. She lives in the East Bay with her partner and two fabulous cats. b535cae3-0a00-47b9-ae40-7fa3e0af7ab5: In Celebration of a Successful Season: performance by Folklórico de Ricardo Velázquez Folklórico de Ricardo Velázquez is more than just a dance academy — it’s a vibrant space where tradition, passion, and pride in our Mexican roots come to life through the art of dance. Our mission is to preserve, celebrate, and pass on the rich cultural heritage of Mexico, honoring our customs, music, and traditional attire with every step and movement rooted in history. This project began just a year ago as a heartfelt dream fueled by dedication and love for our community. Today, we are proud to have grown into a family of over 60 students, ranging in age from four years old and up. Each dancer is a vital part of this artistic family, united by a shared love for our traditions and a commitment to keeping Mexico’s cultural legacy alive for generations to come. Thank you to the Friends of the Oakland Public Library for supporting this program. El Ballet Folklórico de Ricardo Velázquez es mucho más que una academia de baile; es un espacio donde la tradición, la pasión y el orgullo por nuestras raíces mexicanas cobran vida a través de la danza. Nuestra misión es preservar, celebrar y transmitir la riqueza cultural de México, honrando nuestras costumbres, música y trajes típicos mediante cada zapateado y cada movimiento lleno de historia. Este proyecto nació hace un año como un sueño lleno de ilusión y compromiso con nuestra comunidad. Hoy, con mucho orgullo, contamos con más de 60 estudiantes, cuyas edades van desde los 4 años en adelante. Cada alumno es parte fundamental de esta familia artística que sigue creciendo, unida por el amor a nuestras tradiciones y el deseo de mantener viva la herencia cultural mexicana para las futuras generaciones. 1429608c-2362-4a9f-b009-4f0e7a0dd2be: The Father Shore is a sweeping novel about fathers and sons, memory and race, and the dangerous fictions that shape us--inspired by the true story of Eugene Marais, one of history's most extraordinary and forgotten minds. Southern Africa, 1890s. Eugene Marais is a brilliant naturalist and iconoclastic journalist whose evolving theories about memory, addiction, and the hive mind are decades ahead of their time. But when tragedy strikes, he abandons his newborn son and disappears into a remote South African forest--leaving behind his child and his conscience, and embarking on research that will haunt both their lives. Thirty years later, his son Charles--now a professor of ancient Buddhist history at Harvard--discovers that his father's work has been weaponized. University faculty are mining Eugene's research to bolster theories of racial hierarchy, and their ambitions are growing darker by the day. Accompanied by a mysterious Jewish graduate student whose fate is becoming entangled with his own, Charles will make an epic journey across continents to heal his fractured past and stop a sinister plot quietly taking root at the world's most prestigious institution. Set across two interlocking timelines--from the British concentration camps of the Boer War to the rising shadow of the Third Reich and WWII-- The Farther Shore is a heart-breaking, exhilarating novel about memory, love, and identity, and about the vast distances we'll travel to find our way home. "An astonishing reimagining of the life of Eugene Marais, The Farther Shore is as intellectually daring as it is lushly immersive. Seth Fleisher renders history with a decadent richness—each page steeped in atmosphere, obsession, and unease—while excavating the dangerous fictions of race and the seductive machinery of rising fascism. What emerges is not just a portrait of a man, but a mirror held up to our own moment: a world still grappling with identity as both inheritance and invention." —Jamie Ford, NYT bestselling author of Hotel on the Corner of Bitter and Sweet "In a rich and visceral style akin to Abraham Verghese’s Cutting for Stone , this novel asks profound questions about memory and instinct in a cross-continental tale of father and son that is deeply moving and unforgettable. Set mostly in South Africa in the early decades of the 1900s—with that new nation recently ravaged by British concentration camps and twisting toward the ugliest of human beliefs— The Farther Shore tells of Eugene Marais, a real-life doctor and lawyer whose passion was furthering Darwin’s work, and his son, Charles, whom Eugene abandoned after his beloved wife died in childbirth. Charles teaches ancient Buddhist texts at Harvard in the 1930s, when the university is embracing Nazi fascism and researching a mode of social control based on the misuse of Eugene’s studies. On discovering this, Charles must abandon his hard-won independence and journey back to South Africa to meet a father intent on escaping from pain, while he himself finally opens to love." —Janet Benton, author of Lilli De Jong “In this achingly relevant debut novel, Seth Fleisher achieves great magic, embodying continents and centuries. Recalling aspects of The English Patient and A Gentleman in Moscow , this rich exploration introduces a cast of fascinating, complex mortals whose voices are accurate not just to history but to the longings of their flawed hearts.” —EDIE MEIDAV, author of Dogs of Cuba and Crawl Space Seth Fleisher is an American author whose work has appeared in the Bellevue Literary Review , Pearl , the Journal of Anthropological Research , and elsewhere. Based in Berkeley, California, he has worked with the World Bank Group and other NGOs in South Africa, India, and more than 40 other countries, and co-founded a U.S.-based democracy initiative to counter the rising tide of authoritarianism. A former Fulbright scholar in Sri Lanka, Seth did Ph.D. work at Harvard in Buddhist social history, a fellowship at Harvard's Center for the Study of World Religions, and a B.A. in literature at Swarthmore, where he and his wife first met in a Chaucer seminar. The Farther Shore is his first novel. Anna Nordberg is an author and journalist whose essays have appeared in Slate magazine, The Washington Post , The New York Times , and the San Francisco Chronicle . Her debut novel, When She Was Ours, came out this summer. Anna grew up in New York City and now lives in San Francisco with her family. 2f04c748-6e28-465a-bc41-0a69a2adac7b: Language Alchemy: Cultivating Peace and Authenticity in Our Relationships - Workshop & Book Signing Free event · Book signing and refreshments provided What is easy for you to express, and what is hard? In this workshop celebrating the launch of Language Alchemy: The Essential Communication Tool Kit for a Life of Peace, Authenticity, and Meaning , transformative communication expert Alejandra Siroka invites to explore how what you find easy or hard to communicate shapes your relationships, your family, and the world we all live in. The language we speak is something we learned, which means we can learn to communicate differently — moving what now feels impossible to say into the realm of the possible. This is not another workshop that offers contrived communication formulas. Language Alchemy® helps you discover your authentic expression for the benefit of all, so that the way you speak and relate becomes a model for the present and the future. In this workshop you will: • Discover how what you find easy or hard to communicate shapes your life and relationships • Hear an excerpt from the book on maturing our language to match our own growth and development • Leave with a new way of understanding communication as a practice of building meaningful relationships About the book We inherited a language of survival, fear, and competition. For centuries we have been taught to win arguments, defend positions, and prove our worth. That language once helped us survive — now it leads us to divisiveness, superficiality, and a global epidemic of loneliness. Language Alchemy offers a groundbreaking, embodied system for turning the Language of Survival™ into a Language of Interconnectedness™, integrating linguistics, Nonviolent Communication, neuroscience, the behavioral insights of Neuro Linguistic Programming, and ancient Eastern wisdom. Through vivid personal stories, reflective exercises, and eight Language Alchemy Principles, it guides readers to unlearn divisive communication, reconnect to body, emotions, and values as guides for authentic expression, and use language as a vehicle for personal healing and collective evolution. This is the book our conversations — and our world — have been waiting for. Refreshments will be provided. Books will be available for purchase and signing.

A New Play by the San Francisco Neo-Futurists · The San Francisco Neo-Futurists present our latest long-form play, We Bought A Gun!, written and performed by jeb and Willie Caldwell, current and former Artistic Directors of The San Francisco Neo-Futurists, respectively. Set in the Bay Area in 2026, We Bought A Gun! weaves historical, cultural, and personal threads through its central narrative: a couple deciding to buy a gun together for the first time. Intimate and occasionally intense (but never macabre), We Bought A Gun! brings the audience beyond the fourth wall and into the dialogue, inviting a communal exploration of compassion, compromise, pain, and purpose in a country born from violence. What must die in order to birth a new world, who decides, and how do we protect each other in the constant struggle for freedom? A departure from The Infinite Wrench format of 30 plays in 60 minutes, this Beyond-the-Wrench production is a full play that adheres to the theatrical tenants of Neo-Futurism: we are who we are, we are where we are, we are doing what we're doing, the time is now. SHOWTIMES: SUN 11/1 - 5pm SAT 11/7 - 4pm SUN 11/8 - 4pm SAT 11/14 - 4pm SUN 11/15 - 6pm SUN 11/22 - 6pm Logistical notes: Runtime is about 80 minutes and there is no intermission. About the Books: Secrets to Surviving the Toddler Years: award-winning author and mother of four Erin Eileen Leigh offers practical, research-based guidance to help you manage the toddler years with confidence. Inside Secrets to Surviving the Toddler Years, you'll find: - Solutions for sleep struggles and daily power battles with your toddler - Strategies for handling picky eating and mealtime chaos - Advice for travel, transitions, and unpredictable toddler behavior - Encouragement for overwhelmed parents - Tips to prioritize self-care and create daily routines Drawing from research, expert recommendations, and conversations with parents of toddlers-as well as her own experience raising four children-Erin provides realistic direction for overwhelmed parents along with some funny and relatable stories about toddler behavior. Yes, the toddler years are intense and challenging, but with the right approach, you can survive and thrive during the toddler stage. Parenting with an Accent: Through her own stories and interviews with other immigrant families, award-winning journalist Masha Rumer paints a realistic and compassionate picture of what it’s like for immigrant parents raising a child in America while honoring their cultural identities. Parenting with an Accent speaks to immigrant and non-immigrant readers alike, incorporating a diverse collection of voices and experiences to provide an intimate look at the lives of many different immigrant families across the country. With a compelling blend of empirical data, humor, and on-the-ground reportage, Rumer presents interviews with experts on various aspects of parenting as an immigrant, including the challenges of acculturation, bilingualism strategies, and childcare. She visits a children’s Amharic class at an Ethiopian church in New York, a California vegetable farm, a Persian immersion school, and more. Through these stories, she opens a window to a world of parenting unique to multicultural families. Immigrant readers will appreciate Rumer’s gentle message about the kind of ethnic and cultural ambivalence that is born of having roots planted in many different soils, while in these pages non-immigrants get a fly-on-the-wall view of the unique experiences of newcomers. Deeply researched yet personal, Parenting with an Accent centers immigrants and their experiences in a new country—emphasizing how immigrants and their children remain an integral part of America’s story. About the Authors: Erin Eileen Leigh is the author of Secrets to Surviving the Toddler Years (2026) and Navigating the Newborn Months and Beyond (2022), a finalist for the IAN Book of the Year Awards. She is a contributing writer for Her View From Home, Motherly, and BabyCenter. A former attorney and mother of four, Erin also coaches middle school cross country and track & field. Masha Rumer is the author of Parenting with an Accent (Beacon Press), winner of the 2023 Sarton Award for Nonfiction. Her writing about immigrant identity and parenting has appeared in The New York Times, Los Angeles Times, The Washington Post, Literary Hub, Newsweek, and elsewhere. Her newspaper reporting has won awards from the New York Press Association. She is currently working on her first novel.

5330f8cb-3bc8-4e5b-8803-0a4963079f94: An unforgettable and lively author event awaits with beloved humorist David Sedaris and his new book, The Land and Its People: Essays . In this new collection, David Sedaris reflects on what it means to be a foreigner, a brother, a lifelong friend, in essays that are “among the best of his career” (Publishers Weekly, starred review). David will be joined in conversation by Susan Orlean, the author of The Library Book , and the soon-to-be-published Joyride: A Memoir . In The Land and Its People , Sedaris investigates what it means to be a traveler, a brother, a lifelong friend. Trying on the role of caretaker after his boyfriend Hugh’s hip-replacement surgery, he both succeeds and fails. He covers ground with his friend Dawn and challenges her to eat a truck tire. A ambivalent Duolingo bot becomes his unlikely confidante as he attempts to describe his family in a foreign language. Ever adding to his list of “Countries I Have Been To,” he rides a horse named Tequila in Guatemala, buys a bespoke priest’s cassock in Vatican City, and goes on safari in Kenya without taking a single photo. Time takes its toll: scrolling through his address book, he counts those he couldn’t bear to outlive, and realizes how many are already gone. He is bitten by a dog and insulted by a wee train passenger. A woman on the street late at night either sexually harasses him or doesn’t. It’s easy to agree with the lady waving a sign that reads, “Enough Is Enough.” And yet, life holds much to delight in: the massive testicles of a ram, a trip abroad with his sisters, a really excellent reptile video, a pair of well-made cotton underpants. Throughout these essays—at once acerbic and tender, playful and profound—Sedaris shows how much there is to marvel at when you keep your head up and your eyes open, observing with warmth and curiosity our fascinating human species and the lands we inhabit. “It’s classic Sedaris: sharp, shameless, and strangely tender." Oprah Daily “With his laconic delivery, Sedaris lures the reader into believing that the topic under discussion might be unremarkable, a you-and-me-in-this-together moment. But then, given Sedaris’ worldview and world weariness, eventually a knotty twist or spicy dash is delivered with the realization that Sedaris’ land is unparalleled, and its people are peerless. Sedaris fans will be queuing for this, craving new expressions of his signature wit and frankness.” Booklist “Dry, sharp, and delightfully observant…It’s already on my list of books I suspect I’ll read more than once.” Garden & Gun “A new David Sedaris collection is a publishing event.” Literary Hub “A welcome return to form for the much-awarded and much-loved humorist…Sedaris remains a national treasure.” —Kirkus (starred review) David Sedaris is the author of fifteen previous books, including Happy-Go-Lucky, When You Are Engulfed in Flames, and Me Talk Pretty One Day. He is a regular contributor to The New Yorker and BBC Radio 4. In 2019, he was inducted into the American Academy of Arts and Letters. He is the recipient of the Thurber Prize for American Humor, the Jonathan Swift Prize for Satire and Humor, and the Terry Southern Prize for Humor. In less than three years, KATZROAR has emerged as a witch and muse of the psychedelic rock scene. The heartbreak of this loss fueled Avila to devote herself to her music fully, and since she brought the project back in 2024 she has worked with a collective of musicians, released an EP, her second album, over a dozen collabs with 10 different artists, and played all over North America. KATZROAR is both the moniker of Kat the artist and the name of the band. Because of the collective nature, the project carries an element of mystery – you never know exactly who is playing, and every song or performance is different than the one before. Founded by Peaches Christ & Vinsantos in 2003 at the Bridge Theatre, partially as a showcase for their own short films that weren’t getting traction at “legitimate” festivals, the SFUSFF ran under their care for six years until 2008. Now, after 10 years, the festival has found a new home at the 4 Star Theater under the care of Piranha Psychotronica and Kafka X, the maniacal minds behind Media Meltdown Movie Madhouse . The San Francisco Underground Short Film Festival exists to celebrate local, independent filmmaking. We proudly champion the overlooked and underrated, the avant-garde and the alternative, the outrageous, the oddball, and the outlandish. We'll be presenting the silly, subversive, surreal, and strange from all Bay Area filmmakers! Spotlight Sundays: Japanese American Legacies of Resistance from Program | 1–2:30 pm Call to Action | 2:30–3:30 pm All-Inclusive Ticket This Sunday, we are stepping into the historical legacy that inspired OMCA’s latest special exhibition, BeHere / 1942: A New Lens on the Japanese American Incarceration . With opening remarks by OMCA Executive Director Lori Fogarty , we will engage with this present moment in American history with the clarity and learnings of the past. Guest speakers Satsuki Ina and Miya Sommers , who both have personal or familial ties to wartime incarceration, will be joined in conversation by host Joemy Ito-Gates to explore how the shadows of this history led them to paths of anti-imperialist organizing, solidarity anchored in love, and healing work in times of enduring racial injustice. TaikoPeace will close the day with an interactive performance of “Ei Ja Nai Ka,” honoring Japanese American immigrant ancestors of this era and the echoes of their resistance through taiko, dance, and song. Come ready to learn, engage, and connect with one another! Visitors are invited to continue the conversation during a post-program Call to Action gathering . Japanese American Families for Justice , Nikkei Resisters , and Tsuru for Solidarity will facilitate interactive protest art activities and share resources on how to get involved with current campaigns. This program is a part of our exhibition programming for BeHere / 1942: A New Lens on the Japanese American Incarceration , on view through December 27, 2026. About Speakers and Performers Satsuki Ina , PhD, was born in the Tule Lake Segregation Center, a WWII maximum-security prison camp for so-called “disloyal” Japanese Americans during WWII. Her parents answered “No” to the so-called Loyalty Questionnaire and, under duress, renounced their American citizenship. She is co-founder of Tsuru for Solidarity, a project of Japanese American social justice advocates working to support front-line immigrant and refugee communities being targeted today. She is a community trauma consultant and author of The Poet and the Silk Girl: A Memoir of Love, Imprisonment, and Protest ( Heyday Books 2024). She is Professor Emeritus at California State University, Sacramento. Miya Sommers (they/she) is a mixed-race gosei (fifth-generation Japanese American) and a third-generation settler on the territory of xučyun, the ancestral and unceded land of the Chochenyo-speaking Ohlone people, the successors of the sovereign Verona Band of Alameda County. In deepening their understanding of this inheritance and responsibility as a settler at the intersection of the U.S. and Japanese empire, Miya’s political commitments center on building in tandem with movements for collective liberation through their work as an educator and land steward. Joemy Ito-Gates (she/her) is a mother, Ethnic Studies educator, and community activist. She has been a public educator for twenty-three years and is the co-superintendent of the Buddhist Church of Oakland’s Dharma School. She is a core member of the grassroots organization Japanese American Families for Justice and has had writing published in Britt Hawthorne’s Raising Antiracist Children and the newly released Mixed Roots: Writers on Multiracial Identity & Both/And Belonging, edited by Anne Liu Kellor. TaikoPeace , founded by PJ Hirabayashi in 2018, uses Japanese taiko drumming to spread kinetic energy, spiritual vibration, and joy while inspiring positive social change and world peace. “PEACE” stands for her acronym: Partnerships, Empathy, and Creative Empowerment. Her signature composition, “Ei Ja Nai Ka,” performed worldwide, commemorates the first Japanese immigrants to America through taiko drumming, dance, and song. TaikoPeace frequently collaborates with other artists. Currently, 888 Taiko Collective has joined TaikoPeace, uniting drum, dance, and song as expressions of resistance, joy, and solidarity with communities engaged in social justice work. 71e2fddb-72c2-4acd-b1e9-08805607bb10: Please join us for a reading by LeeAnn Pickrell from her new book, Tsunami . This event is organized by the Left Coast Writers and hosted by Book Passage. This story explores the tsunami through a lens of separation, reunion, and the psychic shifts of such an experience. It is a moving account of coming home, letting go of outdated faith, and discovering the connections forged through the stories we tell. On the morning of December 26, 2004, an undersea earthquake struck off the coast of Sumatra in the Indian Ocean. The resulting tsunami killed an estimated 230,000 people across fourteen countries, from Indonesia to Sri Lanka to Thailand to the Maldives to India and all the way to East Africa. Everyone who was there and survived has a story of where they were when the tsunami hit. But there are too many stories that will never be told. This is one woman's story of her experience of that day and its aftermath.LeeAnn Pickrell was in Rai Leh, Thailand, just off the beach drinking coffee that morning when the ocean went away. Everyone ran to the top of the beach to see a wall of white approaching the shore, at first slowly and then picking up speed as boats overturned and they realized the wave wasn't going to stop. It's the story of the tsunami in a particular place, of not understanding what was happening, of separation and reunion. It's also a story of coming home, of not being hurt physically but the psychic shifts of such an experience. It's about letting go of old ideas of faith that no longer make sense and opening to the connections we have to each other through the stories we tell. LeeAnn Pickrell is the author of Tsunami (Unsolicited Press, 2026). Her debut collection, Gathering the Pieces of Days , was published in 2025 by Unsolicited Press. She is also the author of the chapbook Punctuated , published by Bottlecap Press in 2024. She lives in the East Bay with her partner and two fabulous cats. 8d726684-a462-4143-b74b-24aec815a98f: The Bay Area Evolving Ground local group meets regularly at The Alembic to meditate together and explore contemporary Vajrayana. We meet and greet, then start with a short introduction to opening awareness meditation. We sit for 20 minutes, take a break, practice some slow standing meditations together, take a break, and then sit for another 20 minutes. We end with questions and discussion. Opening awareness is a seated meditation leading to vividness and spacious clarity. It is Evolving Ground’s foundational meditation and is a contemporary version of the Dzogchen practice of shi-ne (shamatha in Sanskrit). The movements come from the Sky Realm Series (Nam'khor in Tibetan). These are Dzogchen long-de practices unique to Evolving Ground. They look and feel quite similar to Qi Gong, though they operate on a different principle: discovery of the nonduality of clarity and bliss, through the experience of “tsal”—embodied awareness as non-ordinary sensation. Attendees need no prior experience. There will be plenty of space for questions, reflections, and group exploration of the practices. This meetup is free to attend. Evolving Ground is a global community exploring a transformational path of passionate involvement with the world. Our life-affirming approach empowers creative, effective individuals: people who live with courage, kindness, and grace.

4f4b1c39-1cc4-46e6-af2d-57a34b675daf: In this one-night-only event, Rachel Maddow, the Emmy Award-Winning MS NOW Host and bestselling author, returns to San Francisco for an intimate conversation about her new book, Department of Fate: The Promise, the Power, and the Collapse of America's Most Consequential Institution. Moderated by Kara Swisher, host of On with Kara Swisher and co-host of Pivot. ABOUT DEPARTMENT OF FATE Rachel Maddow leads a revelatory, rollicking trip through the history of the Justice Department, finding heroism and treachery in equal measure—and, in the end, a rescue effort for our battered democracy. Over its nearly 150 years, the United States Department of Justice became America’s most consequential institution, determining the rules and limits of what makes us who we are as a country: our political freedoms, our economy, and our nation’s most revolutionary core principle: equal protection under the law. As the Department made wildly consequential decisions about what types of Americans to target, and for what crimes, it has been steered at times by patriotism, bravery, and self-sacrifice, but just as often by lust for power, corruption, and vengeance. Its political masters have cherrypicked economic winners and losers, determined which causes will be allowed to succeed or fail, and dictated which people and places will thrive and which will be beaten down. The department has fixed the path of the nation’s political swings. In this searing new history, Rachel Maddow traces these triumphs and misdeeds through the founding and rise of the KKK, the riotous chaos of the Red Scare, civil rights murders and violence, railroad barons’ crushing of unions, cabinet scandals that make Watergate look like Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, the faux erudite lawlessness of the Reagan Administration, and the collapse into thug rule in the Trump Administration. Written in her typical whip-smart prose and with a biting sense of clarity, Department of Fate invites us to see how the history of this key institution illuminates a path ahead for a more resilient, re-democratized America committed to making good on even its loftiest promises. In a moment beset with polarization and misinformation, Maddow’s voice shines in this blistering demand to do better—to rebuild the republic, and stronger this time. ABOUT RACHEL MADDOW Rachel Maddow is the Emmy Award and Murrow Award–winning host of The Rachel Maddow Show on MS NOW, as well as the #1 New York Times bestselling author of Drift, Blowout, and Prequel, and the New York Times bestselling co-author of Bag Man. Maddow received a bachelor’s degree in public policy from Stanford University and earned her doctorate in political science at Oxford University. She lives in New York City and Massachusetts with her partner, artist Susan Mikula. Kara Swisher, host of On with Kara Swisher and co-host of Pivot Kara Swisher is host of On with Kara Swisher and co-host of Pivot. She’s editor-at-large at New York Magazine and a CNN contributor, where she hosts the series Kara Swisher Wants to Live Forever. She was the cofounder and editor-at-large of the technology website Recode and co-executive producer of the Code conference. Considered the top reporter in the tech game, Swisher has been reporting on the industry since the early 1990s. She is a former contributing opinion writer for The New York Times and has also worked for The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post. She’s the author of the New York Times–bestselling memoir Burn Book: A Tech Love Story (Simon & Schuster, 2024). Arrive however you are, and leave having touched something vast, intimate, and unknowably alive within you.

Lynne Kaufman ( Playwright ) is the author of 20 full-length plays that have been produced in San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington D.C., and Louisville at such theatres as Magic Theatre, Actors Theatre of Louisville, TheatreWorks Silicon Valley, and many more –with Shameless Hussy being her most recent work which premiered at The Marsh San Francisco spring 2025. Four of Kaufman’s plays, Extreme Acts, Acid Test, Two Minds , Who Killed Sylvia Plath , and Poetic Justice, have premiered on stage at The Marsh, while two others, Exposing Margaret Mead and The Smartest Woman in America, have appeared on The Marsh’s digital platform MarshStream. Who Killed Sylvia Plath went on to win Best Play in The Marsh’s 2020 MarshStream International Solo Festival. Kaufman’s plays have won many awards including the Glickman Award for Best New Play ( The Couch ), the Kennedy Center’s Fund for New American Plays Award ( Speaking in Tongues ), and the Neil Simon Festival New Play Award ( William Blake in Hollywood ). Kaufman has published four novels, and her short stories have appeared in Cosmopolitan , Redbook , and McCall’s . She was also the recipient of the Otis Guernsey Outstanding New Voice in American Theatre Award from the William Inge Theatre Festival. Warren David Keith ( Director ) is delighted to be reunited with Playwright Lynne Kaufman. His work with her began in 2012 with the Marsh Berkeley premier of Acid Test: The Many Incarnations of Ram Dass , a solo piece in which he played the title role. The play was extended twice in Berkeley then transferred for one performance to a massive tent on Maui, Hawaii where it was seen and enjoyed by Ram Dass and about 300 devoted followers. Subsequently, Acid Test opened at the Marsh San Francisco in 2013 where it also had several runs. Keith has acted in theaters throughout the Bay Area, most recently in 1984 at the Aurora Theatre Company and as the Porter in the California Shakespeare Theater’s production of Macbeth . His film credits include Nomadland , The Last Black Man in San Francisco , Haiku Tunnel , Love and Taxes , Raising Arizona , Fargo , A Serious Man , and The Big Lebowski . As a director he mounted more than 15 productions for American Conservatory Theater’s Young Conservatory Program. He reunited with Ms. Kaufman to direct Who Killed Sylvia Plath and The Smartest Woman in America about the final days of Susan Sontag, both at the Marsh San Francisco. Arwen Anderson ( Performer ) returns to The Marsh, where she previously collaborated with Lynne Kaufman on a staged reading of her musical Map of Your Mind and performed in Kaufman’s Extreme Acts . Between them, 2022 NEA Jazz Master Stanley Clarke and 1998 NEA Jazz Master Ron Carter have defined and redefined the bass’s role in modern jazz, from the hard bop innovations of the early 1960s to the jazz-fusion revolution of the 1970s and 1980s. The four-time GRAMMY winning Clarke achieved worldwide fame as a pioneer of jazz fusion with Chick Corea and Return to Forever, and his subsequent career as a bandleader. The Philadelphia native has recorded 24 albums as a leader, leading a procession of masterful bands, and collaborating with George Duke, McCoy Tyner, Dexter Gordon, Freddie Hubbard, Al Di Meola, Paul McCartney, Keith Richards, Stewart Copeland, and dozens more. Ron Carter is, quite simply, the face of jazz bass. A towering figure, he was already a creative force on the roiling early ‘60s scene when he joined Miles Davis in 1962, the first piece of what became the trumpeter’s second great quintet. With more than 2,300 albums to his credit, including over 60 as a leader, "The Maestro” holds the Guinness World Record as jazz’s most recorded bassist. Clarke and Carter collaborated in a trio with guitarist Russell Malone as part of the recent PBS documentary on Carter’s life, Ron Carter: Finding the Right Notes. 4ea647de-6756-4c2a-a6a5-8dcc6f609f4d: It opens with the ephemeral sounds of nature. Birds, bugs, and airy notes chiming in the air. Then, the undercurrent of something darker, disrupting the fantasy: a distorted voice. “To live is to be,” the voice says, “Like the nigga in the tree.” This is how Dark Times , Vince Staples’ eighth studio album, begins. It’s a new era in the prolific artist’s canon, a muscular and revelatory work refining elements that have been present in his catalog for the last decade: dense lyricism over lush, layered beats; wry, melancholic observations about life; finding pockets of light in an endless dark. For Staples, the album is “a snapshot” of this period of his life. “It’s been 10 years since I started putting things out properly,” he says, referencing his first EP, with Def Jam in 2014, Shyne Coldchain Vol 2, “I don’t really keep track of any of that stuff, but it’s important to take a second to appreciate the journey.” The title came intuitively to Staples after he listened to the record in full, noticing heavy motifs that kept reappearing. The album cover, featuring a faintly seen noose, was similarly intuitive. Staples began recording the album over a seven-month stretch, during weekly sessions in North Hollywood . At the time, he was in post-production on his critically acclaimed Netflix series The Vince Staples Show , which he wrote, produced and starred in. Working on the show was “very, very instrumental in how I view creativity,” Staples says. The TV series, an intensely collaborative project that took millions of dollars and hundreds of crew and cast members, was a stark contrast to the way Staples works when he’s recording music. “You can sit by yourself and create it,” he says. “It made me appreciate the simplicity of the process even more.” He maintained that simplicity in various ways, including the decision not to feature other musicians on any of the 13 tracks. “I had a clear vision for the project,” he says of Dark Times. Though Staples has memorable features on past records—such as Kendrick Lamar rapping over a beat by the late Sophie on 2017’s Big Fish Theory—Darkimes felt like a solo journey. Instead, the guest voices on the album are limited to samples, friends popping up in the studio, and a narrative outro by Santigold, the iconic alt singer-songwriter, who tells Staples about an apocalyptic, yet awe-inspiring dream she once had. On the track “Liars,” Staples also includes an iconic excerpt of Nikki Giovanni and James Baldwin in conversation in 1973, debating about Black love. “Lie to me, smile,” Giovanni declares, urging Black men to show Black women respect and care. “That was one of my non-negotiables,” Staples says of having this interlude on the album, inspired by Giovanni’s persistence. “She was very adamant in what she was saying, and she was going to get her point across.” The first release from the album, “Shame on the Devil,” is a perfect introduction to the spirit of Dark Times . For Staples, the song is a personal achievement. “It’s me mastering some things I’ve tried before that I wasn’t great at in the beginning,” he says. “It’s a testament to musical growth, song structure—all the good stuff.” The track features Staples rapping over a warm, spectral beat, ruminating on how anointed his life is now, in spite of bouts of loneliness and fallouts with friends. “Mission complete, out of the mud, labeled a ‘leader” they following cuz,” he raps. “Light on my feet, floating above/I don’t be creeping or keeping in touch.” He’s similarly introspective in “Government Cheese,” rapping about an imprisoned friend who calls him up after seeing him on TV. “Asked how he was/Said he seen me on ABC/Told him that I was good/Wonder if he believed,” Staples raps. A few lines later, Staples talks about the death of his older brother, and how it humbled him, forcing him to reflect on the fragility of life in a new way. Staples balances out the melancholy with celebratory tracks, including “Étouffée,” a bouncy ode to his familial roots in Louisiana, and “Little Homies,” a word of encouragement to the younger generation, the chorus of which flows like a mantra: “Life hard, but I go harder/Streets cold, but the road taught us/Concrete where the rose blossom.” In “Freeman,” the final song before Santigold’s outro, Staples reflects on his life with cool bravado: “It feels good to be a free man with clenched hands/I used to pray to find a way to make a label advance/But nowadays 100K ain’t even getting my glance/Ain’t even setting up no meeting ’til they meet my demands.” But as the song progresses, he drifts into a more zen place: “I understand I’m just a grain of sand and life is a beach/Only heaven knows whichever way I’ll blow in the breeze.” The lines mirror Staples’s entire philosophy about making Dark Times. “It’s a testament to where I am right now and how I view things—it's just a timestamp,” Staples says. “I might not feel like that again tomorrow. But in the process of making this project, these were the things that spoke to me.”

e4127264-ae4a-431d-8f1b-a71d261632f1: Todd Day Wait Todd Day Wait is one of the last real American Workhorse, pedal to the metal, Troubadours by way of Missouri, to California, to New Orleans and now Nashville. The original material of Todd Day Wait, is highly influenced by early American folk, country and blues music from the 1920's through the 1960's, embodying the spirit and authenticity of traditional American music. Todd Day Wait, whom you may have heard of from his millions of spins on GemsOnVHS or WesternAF writes and performs his own style of timeless country music. Harking back to Jimmie Rodgers, Willie Nelson, Wynn Stewart and Kris Kristofferson he keeps the spirit of country music alive. In 2009 he put all his earthly belongings on the curb and hit the road, in his diesel shuttle bus fueled by vegetable oil, for a never ending tour. From busking the streets of New Orleans, to playing in the shadow of European castles, to lighting up the honky-tonk dance floors in Nashville, Todd keeps it 60/50. Bandcamp | IG Mac Cornish Growing up in the shadow of the Santa Cruz mountains in Northern California, Mac spent her days strolling through the redwoods and tracing her footsteps on the grounds of her grandfather's cattle ranch in the North Bay. Such a setting that would provide her with an undying appreciation and respect for all things old in age and of the earth. Mac discovered her love for music digging through her parents' record collection, emerging and adorning herself with not just the tunes, but the entire look and aesthetic of the music Mecca, Laurel Canyon. Drawing inspiration from Linda Ronstadt, Gram Parsons, Jackson Browne and Buffalo Springfield, she began forging her own songs and style from her bouts with love, loss, tragedy and tranquillity. After years away spent in Portland, OR and Nashville, TN, Mac has made her way back to California, where she can be found on the stages of dives and honky tonks, warming the hearts of locals with tales of old pickup trucks and summer drives forever. Inspiring crowds to grab hold of their neighbor, dance and twirl and stomp their feet. When she performs, she pins her heart to her collar and shares her wit and charms that transcend the stage and grab hold of the hearts of all who bear witness. cfe236ce-7aac-4897-a1fd-1b96222333ac: Over the past two decades, Nick Paumgarten has become one of The New Yorker’s most admired staff writers, bringing an instinct for character and complexity to journalism. His memoir, The Intangibles , offers a mordant anthropology of sports that explores and undermines the mythologies of manhood. Over the past two decades, Nick Paumgarten has become one of the New Yorker ’s most admired and popular staff writers. He brings to journalism what great novelists bring to fiction: an instinct for character, a respect for complexity, and an eye for the telling moment. THE INTANGIBLES: Friendship, Fatherhood, and the Love of the Game (on sale November 10; Penguin Press) is Paumgarten’s first book, a memoir told through the oddly illuminating lens of hockey. Not a book about hockey, really, but one in which a lifetime of obsessively hanging around the game—as player, parent, son, coach, fan, middle-aged white guy in New York, person of privilege, an imperfect man among other imperfect men—provides a window into a cultish world that hides in plain sight. It’s an alternate realm of aspirational vigor and prolonged boyishness, of plucky brutishness and occasional violence, a haven and release from the pressures of adulthood and city life. In THE INTANGIBLES—the name of Paumgarten’s beer league team—we meet an array of hockey-crazy men, the author included, trying to make their way through the world with the baggage that’s been laid on them by the men who came before them, and the growing knowledge that they have laid their own baggage on their sons. A sharp, witty, and ultimately introspective exploration of masculinity—of boys and men, sons and fathers, of both the toxic and non-toxic kinds—the book is a deep, questioning look at a certain world of male friendship, in which sports become the common language for a group of men who otherwise might not have one. Paumgarten’s memoir both explores and undermines some of the mythologies of manhood and sports. In doing so he’s created a portrait of men at play, undertaking a kind of competitive pursuit that defies logic, age, orthopedics, and the responsibilities of grown-up life. A mordant anthropology of hockey and its tribe, THE INTANGIBLES is unlike anything else you’ve read. “Just ridiculously good. Line for line, the richest, funniest book I’ve read in years. Only Nick Paumgarten could turn beer league hockey into spun gold. It’s the examined life on skates. Friendships so deep and unlikely, all the unspoken codes, the writer’s raw honesty with himself, the vestigial violence between grown men. I did not want it to end.” — William Finnegan, Pulitzer-Prize winning author of Barbarian Days “When I finished this book, I experienced many different emotions at once. I felt deeply unsettled, filled with both melancholy and triumph, mixed with feelings of admiration and envy for the beautiful writing and the howitzer power of the details, and with the sense that I’d finally read the sports story I’ve been waiting for my whole life. I loved this book, clearly, but more important, I get it. How this was a story Nick Paumgarten must tell, a story he’d been preparing, byline by byline, to write for his whole life. I understood his lofty ambitions, how he wanted to create a lush tapestry in which his teammates — in which he and his father and his sons — could strive towards the only real job for a man: to take what we inherited and pass on the good, and try to understand and prune the bad, and to find our place on a wheel that is turning and can’t slow down. To know ourselves before we return to dust. In the end his outsized ambitions are matched, then surpassed, by the way the book lingers emotionally after the last sentence like the echoes of a siren or train horn in an empty midnight hockey barn.” — Wright Thompson, bestselling author of The Barn and senior writer at ESPN “ Two of the greatest sports books of all time are Ken Dryden’s elegant, elegiac The Game and Jim Bouton’s raucous, irreverent Game Four . The Intangibles is their concussed offspring—brilliantly written, hilarious, insightful, unsparing, humane, moving in the extreme. Did I say sports book? This is simply a great book, one that will stay with me.” — Louisa Thomas, staff writer at The New Yorker “Nick Paumgarten’s marvelous memoir The Intangibles is itself filled with so many intangibles that they are impossible to catalogue. There is the charm, the wit, the poignant coming-of-age story, the laugh-out-loud lines, the mad beer-league hockey scenes, the violence, the grace, the messiness of life, the insights into parenthood, the moments of transcendence. What they all add up to is something tangible: one of the best books I’ve read this year, or any other.” — David Grann, #1 New York Times bestselling author of The Wager and Killers of the Flower Moon “I don’t care one bit about hockey, and yet I couldn’t put this book down and didn’t want it to end. Nick Paumgarten has written the rare book about men that is also, secretly, a book about love: the strange, tender, often ridiculous ways men love each other and their sons. The Intangibles is a book to be read and savored by everyone.” — Susan Orlean, New York Times bestselling author of Joyride Nick Paumgarten has been a staff writer at the New Yorker since 2005. Prior to that, he spent five years as an editor and writer at the magazine. He has covered a wide range of subjects, including politics, finance, art, music, food, technology, mountaineering, sports-talk radio, elevators, boxer-bartenders, commuters, and canoes. His work has also appeared in Outside , GQ , Bon Appetit , Men's Vogue , Powder , the Adventure Journal , and The Sewanee Review . He was an editor and reporter at the New York Observer from 1995-2000. He lives with his wife Siv in Manhattan. Cha Chaan Teng- Chef, writer, culinary educator, and Food & Wine Best New Chef: 2021, Lucas Sin writes his debut cookbook on Hong Kong-style comfort food. The cha chaan teng―Hong Kong's iconic neighborhood diner―is where the city has always fed itself. Born from the collision of Chinese cooking, Western influence, and a century of migration and colonial exchange, the restaurants serve everyone from day laborers to schoolchildren, and the food is some of the most beloved in the world: Baked Pork Chop Rice and Beef Chow Fun, Pineapple Buns and Coconut Tarts, Milk Tea, Red Bean Ice, and more. Lucas Sin has spent years documenting the food of Hong Kong’s cha chaan teng with the rigor of an anthropologist and the instincts of a cook, learning these recipes from the chefs who've spent careers refining them. The result is 128 recipes of comfort food made with the same eye for detail as anything in a fine-dining kitchen. These are some of the most satisfying dishes you’ll ever make: crisp, custardy egg tarts, three variations of Hong Kong-style French toast, and stir-fries with real wok hei. Cha Chaan Teng is the ultimate collection of Hong Kong’s favorite food ― affordable, generous, and unfettered in its deliciousness.

303809e6-860a-4509-95d8-7d1e95103aec: A conversation about Fiona McPhillips' new novel, The Party in the Woods · In this conversation, Irish journalist, screenwriter, and author Fiona McPhillips will join New York Times bestselling author Cara Black to discuss the journey behind McPhillips’ sophomore novel, The Party in the Woods. Exporing gender inequality, class divides, motherhood, marriage, adult friendships, and power, McPhillips and Black will examine the Irish rave scene of the early 2000s and its lasting impact on Irish culture. Their conversation will also address what it means to outgrow decades-old relationships, the consequences of sacrificing career ambitions for domesticity, and how the grief of those losses can emerge and resurface over time. Their discussion will also offer insight into how McPhillips threads the needle between research into Ireland’s historical class barriers and ongoing housing crisis and her own experience as an Irish-born rave DJ. By exploring how these influences inform the novel’s characters and their circumstances, McPhillips will illuminate the complexities of their lives on the page and the very real, sometimes dire realities they face. Fiona McPhillips is an Irish journalist, author and screenwriter, and an editor at The Forge literary magazine. Fiona's debut novel, When We Were Silent, was shortlisted for the Irish Book Awards, runner-up for the Crime Writers' Association Debut Dagger and named as one of the Irish Times' crime books of the year. The Party in the Woods is her second novel. Cara Black is the author of twenty-one books in the New York Times bestselling Aimée Leduc Paris based series as well as the WWII thrillers Three Hours in Paris and Night Flight to Paris and Huguette, historical fiction. She has won the Médaille de la Ville de Paris and the Médaille d’Or du Rayonnement Culturel.

5f99163e-0b39-4e2e-b4b6-ca7ba62cb68e: 🦠 What did the very first living thing on Earth actually look like? One of the most profound questions in biology is also one of the simplest: what is life? A powerful way to approach it is to trace life's origins back to LUCA, the Last Universal Common Ancestor. Although LUCA lived billions of years ago, microbiologists can infer many of its properties by studying the extraordinary diversity of microorganisms alive today, including both bacteria and archaea. In this talk, Dipti Nayak, Assistant Professor at UC Berkeley, explores what scientists currently know about LUCA and the early evolution of life on Earth, and how researchers have pieced these insights together through the study of modern microbial diversity. Archaea, a profoundly important yet often overlooked group of microorganisms, play a starring role in this story. Nayak's talk offers a window into how life originated, how it continues to evolve on our planet, and what that might mean for the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. 🔬 🕰 Event Details What should I expect? 7:00-7:35 --> arrival & chats 7:35-8:20 --> lecture 8:20-9:00 --> q&a and more chatting Who's invited? Fiona McPhillips is an Irish journalist, author and screenwriter, and an editor at The Forge literary magazine. Fiona's debut novel, When We Were Silent, was shortlisted for the Irish Book Awards, runner-up for the Crime Writers' Association Debut Dagger and named as one of the Irish Times' crime books of the year. The Party in the Woods is her second novel. Cara Black is the author of twenty-one books in the New York Times bestselling Aimée Leduc Paris based series as well as the WWII thrillers Three Hours in Paris and Night Flight to Paris and Huguette, historical fiction.
