9d395710-43c2-4beb-81e2-2c09a78c0914: Bookshop West Portal cannot wait to host renowned science fiction author of the Mars trilogy, The Ministry for the Future , and The High Sierra: A Love Story, and lifelong advocate for the wilderness and the environment, Kim Stanley Robinson. Join us to celebrate his new book, The Best Journey in the World: An Antarctic Story , a gripping story of adventure that brilliantly intertwines memoir and polar history. Learn about one of the most perilous places on our planet, how it shaped out history, and it’s importance for our future. You won't want to miss the truly stunning never-before-seen photography either! This event is FREE to attend. Seating is first-come, first-served. (RSVPs are optional, but encouraged for our planning purposes.) About the Book: Interweaving memoir, some never-before-published photographs, and good old fashioned ice adventure, Kim Stanley Robinson takes readers along on the Arctic journeys that have happened before and the journeys that may never happen again. In May of 1911, Robert Scott and the twenty-four men under his command said good-bye to the sun and settled in for the long Antarctic winter. When the sun returned in September, they were going to try to become the first people to reach the South Pole. However, a week past the winter solstice, Scott's second-in-command took a team on a trip to Cape Crozier to man-haul two sledges through the perpetual night of the Antarctic winter, exposed to the coldest temperatures human beings had ever traveled in. This side trip was, at best, a dangerous distraction and at worst, a disaster. Yet, chronicled by zoological assistant (and major expedition funder) Apsley Cherry-Garrard, it became The Worst Journey in the World , one of the best adventure books ever written. Kim Stanley Robinson first read Cherry-Garrard's book in his twenties and re-read it again in 1995, as part of his preparations to Antarctica that he made that year as research for his Mars novels. It was a dream excursion: he traveled around the continent, by snowmobile and helicopter and airplane. All the while, Cherry's book loomed larger and larger in Robinson's mind, and he tried to follow in their ill-fated footsteps. Ultimately, in The Best Journey in the World , we see Robinson stepping on ice and finding an earthly holy place. As he searches for what can--and cannot--be found again, he takes readers on a journey of realization that is not just about being the first to get somewhere but about falling in love with what the world has to offer us. That being with people who also feel a kinship to a place worthy of preserving is itself, an act of devotion. Replete with gorgeous photographs taken in a place many will never set foot, and woven throughout with Robinson's sharp, funny, and personal voice, prepare to take the best journey in the world. One of the New Yorker's Most Anticipated Fall Reads About the Author: Kim Stanley Robinson is the author of more than twenty books, including the bestselling Mars trilogy, The Ministry for the Future , and The High Sierra: A Love Story . He was a featured speaker at COP26 in Glasgow, at the UN’s Summit of the Future in 2024, and at COP30 in Belém, Brazil. His work has been translated into thirty languages, and in 2016 asteroid 72432 was named Kimrobinson. He lives in Davis, California.

A Night of Gospel Brilliance, Soul & Praise · Join us for an unforgettable night of Gospel, Soul, and Praise as we usher in the holiday season with the angelic voice of gospel singer-songwriter Sylvia Anderson and her anointed guest, Grammy Award winner Darrel Walls, gospel legend Derrick Hall, and the music direction and ministry of Carl Wheeler. An inspiring evening of deliverance, celebration, and worship you won’t want to miss. Presented by Sylvia Anderson & Mark Elliott of the A-list Musiq Circle - Your Bay Area Who's Who Entertainment network. With Special Guest Host TBA. A gifted gospel artist with an angelic voice and a heart devoted to ministry, Sylvia Anderson has spent over 40 years using her God-given talent to inspire, uplift, and spread the love of Jesus Christ. Born into a family rich in musical and spiritual heritage, her journey began at the tender age of five when she discovered her ability to sing. Guided by her father, a preacher and singer, and her mother, a vocalist, she was nurtured in a household where music and faith were inseparable. She first sang with the Coleman Sisters, under the influence of her father, Willie Coleman, and continued to grow musically, sharing her voice with groups such as Derrick Hall & Company and the Center of Hope Choir. Her remarkable gift has also led her to sing background for gospel greats, including Tramaine Hawkins and Nona Brown, and appear on BET’s renowned Bobby Jones Gospel Hour. A true musician, she’s sung in concerts, gospel festivals, weddings, homegoing services and private events, further enhancing her ability to minister through music. In addition to her musical journey, she has served faithfully in ministry and is currently a minister at Covenant Worship Center in Berkeley, California. Beyond the stage, she is deeply committed to serving her community. She holds a Bachelor’s degree in Theology and is the owner of a care home for children, as well as actively involved in foster care initiatives—demonstrating her passion for nurturing and uplifting the next generation. A woman of many roles, she is a devoted mother of three, a loving wife, grandmother, sister, and friend. For over 30 years, she has also worked as a professional hairstylist, touching lives both inside and outside the church, and retired after 33 years from the medical field. Rooted in Oakland, California, her life’s mission is simple yet powerful: to send God’s love through every song, every act of service, and every life she encounters. Her favorite song, “Because He Lives,” reflects the foundation of her faith and the message she carries wherever she goes. Darrel Walls is the eldest sibling and eldest member of The Walls Group, the acclaimed four-sibling group celebrated for their distinctive harmonies, musicianship, and progressive sound. A gifted vocalist, musician, and creative force, Darrel has long been an integral part of the group’s unmistakable musical identity. Stepping into his own as a solo artist, he recorded his debut solo project, Heart of Mine, with Grammy-winning artist and producer PJ Morton, earning the 2026 Grammy Award for Best Gospel Album. His breakout solo season has continued with three Stellar Award wins, including Artist of the Year and Contemporary Male Artist of the Year, while his single “ABLE” reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Gospel Airplay chart. His solo journey has further established him as one of gospel music’s standout voices. While continuing to bring his unmistakable sound to The Walls Group, Darrel is building an exciting solo legacy of his own.

aec56b7f-b348-4285-ae42-cb8cf8282a47: Experience the deep benefits of Zhineng (Wisdom Healing) Qigong. This practice strengthens the immune system, supports the body’s natural capacity to heal, and cultivates mental clarity and emotional steadiness. Through simple, time-honored movements, the nervous system unwinds, the mind becomes more spacious, and the heart opens. Over time, practitioners often feel more resilient, centered, and connected — both inwardly and outwardly. Tickets are sliding scale $10-$25 - Please arrive at least 5-10 minutes early. Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. About the Book Everyone's favorite TV and podcast host is back ... with a vengeance. After realizing that every win in her life came right after being underestimated, rejected, or told she wasn't enough, Keltie Knight decided to build a theory around it: The F*ck Them Theory. Part memoir, part manifesto, The F*ck Them Theory is your permission slip to stop apologizing and start transforming rejection into power. It's not about bitterness, it's about alchemy. She shares raw, unfiltered stories from behind the curtain--the breakdowns, the pills, the plastic surgery, the feud the tabloids never caught, and the family secrets she's never shared ... until now. The F*ck Them Theory is for anyone who's been underestimated or is tired of being "grateful for the opportunity" when they deserved so much more. About the Author Keltie Knight is a three-time Emmy Award–winning television personality, New York Times bestselling author, and People’s Choice Award–nominated podcast host. She currently hosts E! Her fashion and cultural influence have been featured in Vogue, Elle, and The New York Times. Keltie spearheaded and created LADYWORLD, the first-ever podcast festival dedicated to female voices, bringing together over 3,000 attendees and generating more than $1M in brand partnerships. Positioned at the forefront of innovation in the female podcast space, she continues to develop new formats that expand how audiences experience content, community, and live events. A sought-after content creator and brand ambassador, Keltie has developed long-term partnerships with brands such as Marshalls and Fabletics, consistently translating audience trust into high-performing, multi-platform campaigns. Her first full length solo book "The F*CK Them Theory: Self-Help For People Who are Done Being the Bigger Person was released through Blackstone Publishing Nov. 2026. In addition to her on-air work, Knight is an investor and advisor to ALTA, an AI-powered fashion technology platform recently named to Time’s 100 Best Inventions of the Year, recognized by Vogue as a Best Invention, and announced as an official AI fashion partner of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA). b83aa747-754b-4413-8529-655ec9242313: Mac Dre. Too $hort. E-40. These are some of the names that come to mind when you think of Bay area rap. Now, San Francisco native, Gilbert Milam Jr., better known in the rap game simply as, Berner, has his eye set at being the next great artist to put on for the Bay. Starting off participating in rap battles at local coffee shops and open mic nights in the San Francisco area in 2007, Berner took things to the next level by turning his passion into his career. This story truly embodies every aspect of the phrase “grassroots.” After creating his own label, Bern One Entertainment, Berner soon after released his debut album, “Track Money & Pack Money,” a joint effort with fellow Bay Area rapper, Equipto. A true testament to his never-ending grind, Berner has released 10 independent albums, several of which have charted on Billboard’s “Top Rap Albums” chart. In March 2012, Berner teamed up with Wiz Khalifa and signed to his Taylor Gang Records, joining the thriving roster which includes the likes of Chevy Woods, Juicy J, Lola Monroe, Courtney Noelle, Tuki Carter and more. “Urban Farmer,” Berner’s first collection to be released on Taylor Gang Records, was released on October 2, 2012 and quickly took the Internet by storm. “Urban Farmer” captures the essence of Bay Area rap on tracks such as “Shut Up (feat. Chris Brown & Problem).” With an impressive list of artist collaborations on his resume, ranging from rap legends Bun B and Wyclef to Chris Brown, Curren$y and even fellow Taylor Gang members Wiz Khalifa and Juicy J, Berner is showing no signs of slowing down in the near future. In fact, he’s just getting started. Always one to master multiple entrepreneurial ventures, Berner isn’t stopping at just music. He has two lifestyle/street clothing lines in the works with “FreshKo” and “Cookies,” as well as his own line of hemp water, appropriately titled “H20.” All told, Berner is letting actions speak louder than words as he is on his way to becoming the future of the Bay Area rap scene. And he’s making sure you hear him, loud and clear.

Rather than a traditional cabaret performance, audiences will experience the stories behind the music through conversation, rare archival video, and curated listening as Russ and Terese revisit the friendships, recording sessions, and memories that shaped the original album and the remarkable journey that led to its newly expanded and remastered 20th Anniversary Edition. The evening culminates in a special presentation of the newly reimagined recording of Christmas in San Francisco. Guests at Feinstein's will be among the first anywhere to hear this beautiful new version. There could be no more fitting place to celebrate its next chapter than the city that inspired it. cf259e5b-4a75-49a1-8df7-df1aedef022b: This richly illustrated lecture* will take us into a world of ocean navigation largely unknown to the West, a world in which the traditional navigator’s only directional tools are the stars, the ocean swells and the flight paths of birds. In 1983 and 1984 I spent eleven months on Satawal Island and in the Western Carolines as an apprentice to Mau Piailug, then one of the last paliuw, captains fully initiated in the Talk of Navigation, the closely guarded, ancient practices around reading the cosmos and the seas. I chronicled my experiences and the navigational techniques in the book The Last Navigator, first published in 1987, and a documentary film of the same title for PBS in 1988. Now some forty years on I have updated the stories with a new generation of Satawalese islanders and researchers in the revised and fully illustrated edition of The Last Navigator. *Original photographs and film footage, 1983-1987 The classic account of traditional Micronesian navigation and “the last navigator,” Mau Piailug, who fought to preserve it—now available in a revised edition illustrated in full color As a young man piloting a small sailboat across the Pacific, Steve Thomas developed a fascination with ancient methods of navigation. He learned that, for thousands of years, the peoples of Oceania had sailed unerringly across the Pacific without compass or charts, guided only by natural signs—stars, waves, and the flight paths of birds. In search of this secret knowledge, Thomas traveled to the tiny island of Satawal in Micronesia, home to Mau Piailug, one of the few surviving paliuw , or navigators. In The Last Navigator , Thomas tells how he convinced Piailug to accept him as his student and teach him the closely guarded Talk of Navigation. It is a remarkable book, offering at once a clear and precise account of Micronesian wayfinding and the moving story of one man trying to preserve his culture against the tide of modernity. Now, forty years after his original journey to study under Mau Piailug, Thomas has worked with a new generation of researchers, including natives of Satawal, to prepare this revised edition of The Last Navigator . All Satawalese words are rendered in the now-accepted orthography, and the islanders, originally identified by pseudonyms, appear under their true names. And throughout, Thomas has added a generous selection of color photographs from his time on Satawal, documenting the island, its people, and its seafaring culture. This result is a lasting tribute to the spirit of the Satawalese, and to the Talk of Navigation A fascinating exploration of a remoted archipelago and its seagoing people — Peter Matthiessen If you have any interest in the sea and navigation or in the impact of colonialism on indigenous cultures, or if you just enjoy a well-told story of adventure, then read on. — from the foreword by David Barrie [Thomas] is a dual explorer, simultaneously trying to rediscover an ancient system of sailing, using only nature’s navigational signals, and trying to find himself in the myth-made culture of Micronesia. . . . [This] is a travel book with a dream. — Los Angeles Times Book Review This is a story of adventure, and coming of age. It is also an important document, preserving an ancient oral tradition. — San Francisco Chronicle Steve Thomas is familiar to television viewers as the two-time Emmy award-winning host of This Old House, Renovation Nation, and Save Our History. But he is also an experienced home builder and sailor. Beginning in 1977, he sailed a 43-foot wooden sloop from England to San Francisco via the Panama Canal, Galapagos, Marquesas, and Hawaii. In the early 1980’s, he journeyed to the remote Micronesian island of Satawal to learn the ancient technique of star path navigation, an experience that resulted in this book as well as a documentary for the PBS series Adventure. A throwback to family reads of yore, this epic follows a troubled boy and a host of hilariously vexed animals who must save a river before it’s dammed, so they can save themselves. Gabriel (“G” for short) is wasting away in the Abiddon County Juvenile Center when he’s introduced to the Shongunk River by his dying uncle. The river valley—trash-heaped but chock-full of mysteries and fish—wins G over. But, as G has learned, good things can’t last. The Shongunk is scheduled to be dammed by a local developer. In a matter of days, it will cease flowing, and all of the talkative creatures who live there in the river valley will be as homeless as G. Just as G decides it’s no time to accept his fate, so too do the animals. To inspire an uprising, a young trout is nominated to make a fateful journey up the river; a raccoon swears a violent oath against humans; and a newly sober buck leads his skittish flock out of harm’s way. Together with G, they show that good can triumph and that there is power in all of us, even the smallest minnow. KIRK LOMBARD is an author, angler, sustainable fishmonger, and tuba player who once worked inside the juvenile rehabilitation system. His gift to audiences during the holidays, ‘The Jewelry Box,’ offers a treasure chest of wit, warmth, and wisdom… Every word counts in Copeland’s masterful 70-minute show… He presents a brilliant array of lovable characters—with warmth and compassion. Copeland weaves them all into a heartwarming show, creating an instant classic, an American ‘Christmas Carol.’” —Barry David Horwitz, Theatrius A holiday memoir about hope, faith and Christmas miracles. It’s December of 1970 in East Oakland and six year old Brian Copeland wants to make his mother smile with a brand new jewelry box for Christmas. How can he possibly raise the needed $11.97 by Christmas Eve? Follow the hilarious, poignant journey of a determined child as he navigates the winos, mean landlords and shady used car salesmen of his rough urban neighborhood, as well as his abusive father to discover the true meaning of the season. Brian Copeland (performer) has been in show business since he first stepped on the comedy stage at the tender age of 18. Soon he was headlining clubs and concerts across the country and opening for such artists as Smokey Robinson, The Temptations, Ringo Starr, and the Queen of soul Aretha Franklin, in venues from The Universal Amphitheater to Constitution Hall in Washington DC. Soon, Copeland branched off into television, appearing on comedy programs on NBC, A&E and MTV. He spent five years as co-host of San Francisco FOX affiliate KTVU breakfast program Mornings on 2 and two years hosting San Francisco ABC affiliate KGO’s Emmy Award winning afternoon talker 7Live. In 1995, ABC affiliate KGO Radio premiered “The Brian Copeland Show”. Its unique mix of talk and entertainment soon made it the most listened to program in its time slot. Copeland branched out into theater in 2004 with his first solo play, NOT A GENUINE BLACK MAN. This critically acclaimed exploration of race and identity created an audience pleasing blend of laughter, tears and sociology that led to the show becoming the longest running solo play in San Francisco theatrical history. Successful runs in Los Angeles and Off Broadway and a bestselling book adaptation followed. GENUINE has been performed in over 30 cities across America. Copeland’s other theatrical work includes THE WAITING PERIOD, a solo play about his lifelong struggle with depression and Grandma & Me, which premiered in 2022 at The Marsh. David Ford (director) is a director, collaborator, and Goldie Award-winning playwright who has worked on countless solo shows over his 25-year career in the business. Frequently working on projects at The Marsh, Ford has collaborated with many Bay Area favorites including Charlie Varon, Marilyn Pitman, Geoff Hoyle and Cherry Terror.

7568d7b0-1f3e-47d0-acf1-58a1de7fa74b: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: Dagmar Zuniga Nicaraguan-American artist Dagmar Zuniga makes music that feels both intimate and expansive: songs drift like disrupted signals, carried by harmony, tape hiss, and a strong sense of touch. Her debut solo album in filth your mystery is kingdom / far smile peasant in yellow music — written and recorded in New York, Norway, and Athens, Georgia over a period of five years on her longtime companion, the Tascam 424 — was released by the People’s Coalition of Tandy on Bandcamp & YouTube in January 2025, accompanied by a small tape run that sold out instantly. The project quickly garnered over two hundred thousand views and the attention of artists such as Mount Eerie, who invited her to tour with them that summer. This year, what was once a jewel of tapped-in algorithms and message boards will meet the world at large, with in filth arriving digitally on March 4 , and physically on April 10 , via AD 93 . in filth is an atmospheric, devotional collage where one voice multiplies into a chorus of selves, sometimes delicate, sometimes severe; an effect created by Zuniga’s masterful layering of texture and complex harmonies. Synths glitter out like spears of sunlight from beneath clouds of moody, time-distorted guitars, and songs spin about themselves like tightly-wound music boxes, making use of a kind of hypnotic repetition, before melting apart into their components or slipping into the following track. Zuniga began recording to tape as a teenager, drawn to the physicality of the medium — how a tape recording is fragile, mutable, and alive. Though her ethereal sound may draw easy comparisons to other female pioneers of psychedelic folk, she is influenced just as much by the darker sounds of Syd Barrett and The Fall. Like Barrett, Zuniga is a painter, and she is interested not only in recording music but in creating a full, self-contained artistic universe: she creates her own artwork, merchandise, music videos, and bootleg tapes of new and unfinished music that she exclusively sells at live shows ( “If something is not material, it does not exist,” she insists). Her world has not gone unvisited, garnering her a monthly show on NTS Radio ‘World of Pain’, as well as a forthcoming appearance at Rewire Festival in April 2026. Though Zuniga’s work explores themes of solitude and suffering, the suffering in her songs is not borrowed or displayed; it is held, then opened outward through empathy — an exacting practice of attention that insists on shared ground. Solitude, in her work, is not withdrawal but a starting point for connection. Likewise, over time, her recording process has become increasingly communal, with in filth featuring musicians across the globe. Newer recordings widen the circle even more. For Zuniga, collaboration is a way to “find a place between worlds,” echoing Badiou’s idea of love as a vision refracted through the prism of difference. Meaning emerges there — in the space between voices, between artist and listener. “I hope my music helps people work through difficult experiences,” she says. “The same way it helps me.” Bandcamp | IG Support to be announced DOORS at 7:00PM | MUSIC at 8:00 PM Tickets

9ae38d6e-2189-4135-9c90-4d42a85e9ae5: A joyful, mischievous, heartfelt book for children and the grown-ups who love them. Recommended for ages 6–10, parents, grandparents, teachers, and anyone who wants to remember what it feels like to live with curiosity, courage, humor, and heart. The Braunicles invite readers into the wonderfully imperfect world of a spirited little boy named Braun. A world filled with adventure, mischief, big feelings, unexpected lessons, and an irresistible enthusiasm for life. Written by Jennifer Levi, the stories are warm, funny, honest, and deeply human. Jennifer gives a distinctive voice and captures childhood in a way that feels both whimsical and completely real: the bold ideas, the questionable decisions, the enormous emotions, the funny family dynamics, and the little moments that often become the memories we treasure most. At its heart, The Braunicles is about living fully. Braun approaches the world with curiosity. He takes chances. He includes people. He makes mistakes. He loves fiercely. He finds fun where others might not see it. And through each story, young readers discover that some of the qualities that make a child challenging, surprising, loud, adventurous, or different can also become their greatest strengths. For parents and grandparents, there is another layer. These stories are a gentle reminder not to rush through childhood trying to make everything perfect. Sometimes the mess is the memory. Sometimes the mischievous child becomes the unforgettable adult. Sometimes the moments that make us shake our heads today are exactly the stories we will tell for the rest of our lives. Jennifer’s voice brings humor and perspective to parenting without preaching. That makes The Braunicles more than a children’s book. -It is a book children can enjoy for adventure. -It is a book parents can recognize themselves in. -It is a book grandparents can give with meaning. -And it is a book families can read together and talk about long after the final page. Jennifer Levi is the founder of The Live Like Braun Foundation and the force behind The Live Like Braun movement. Since the death of her son in May 2025, Jennifer has become a powerful advocate for DUI awareness and meaningful legislative change, passing a new Bill in CA, testifying at the CA State Capitol and on Capitol Hill. She regularly speaks to audiences at DUI workshops and schools all over Southern CA. She serves on MADD's CA State Legislative Board. Jennifer’s advocacy has been featured across multiple media outlets and television networks including NBC, ABC, Fox, and CBS, along with well-known podcasts hosted by Dr. Phil, Kennedy, Jason Kennedy, Amanda Kloots, Kelly Gores, Meghan Judge, and Kate Casey. Jennifer has spoken openly about the profound transformation of her life following the death of her son. She has become a featured contributor to Maria Shriver’s Sunday Paper, writing about the ways grief has reshaped her life with raw honesty, deep emotion, and a touch of irreverence. She hopes The Braunicles inspires children to embrace exactly who they are and encourages grown-ups to give young people the freedom to let their brightest, silliest, most authentic selves shine. Jennifer is a mother, wife, advocate, writer, and former TV executive. Although she has worn many hats, she has always said she is most proud of her role as mom to her two children, Adelle and Braun. She lives in Pacific Palisades, California, with her family and two very naughty dogs. 7feec097-83ec-4c20-a9b2-2083ae6d7bae: Many of us work with psychedelics without a guide or with limited support to integrate these experiences. That can feel painful or lonely when we’ve had meaningful journeys (and also when we’ve had disappointing journeys!). Healing – especially from interpersonal injuries – deepens when done in community. The same is true of personal and spiritual growth. Even the most joyful experiences are best metabolized when witnessed. Together, we become a mosaic – a colorful and varied community, greater together than the sum of our parts. Mosaic is a psychedelic integration circle for self-identified women. Here, you’ll find a supportive space to integrate the lessons, challenges, and wisdom from psychedelic journeys so that you can apply those learnings to everyday life. The at times humorous and at times deadly serious show begins when Amy moves to Berkeley in the early 1970’s during second wave feminism. Amy finds her identity as a lesbian feminist, goes to law school to fight for women’s rights, represents coal miners and battered women in Appalachia and returns to California to open a lesbian feminist law practice. She is representing women who had been sexually harassed – pre-Anita Hill – but keeps seeing all sides of things, becomes an administrative judge and starts a law firm to do mediation and impartial investigations of harassment and discrimination. She adopts two children – both biracial – and experiences racism up close and personal. In the meantime, she can’t stop revisiting her first experience with the criminal justice system in 1970 when she accompanied a friend to a rape trial. Her (white) friend had been raped by a (Black) boyfriend. The friend wanted him to get help, rather than serve a decade in prison. This restorative justice solution was not an option. Amy wonders about her role in the verdict and if real justice is possible in an unjust world. Immersing himself in the West Coast underground DIY community in the mid-2000s, Steinbrink left on his first tour at the age of sixteen and continued performing internationally for a decade, living an improvised existence and recording incessantly. He has released nine critically acclaimed albums of experimental pop music and has collaborated as a producer and session player with artists including Boy Scouts/Taylor Vick, Dear Nora, Gia Margaret, LAKE, and Girlpool. Though appearing luminous and graceful on the surface, his songs use the recognizable logic of pop structures as a container for psychic inquiry, revealing the unstable landscapes of memory, dreams, and the quotidian absurdities of daily life. Over two decades, Steinbrink has become one of the most distinctive songwriters on the U.S. West Coast, with a rarely matched gift for poetic imagery carried by a musical language that moves across folk, experimental pop, and ambient experimentation. In visual art, Steinbrink works in illustration, photography, animation, and Stained Glass conservation, having restored historic art glass throughout Northern California. He currently lives and works in Oakland, California. 9ce758cf-5dc4-408b-a89d-dc13e5067980: Making sense of a holiday tradition. · When it first premiered in St. Petersburg in 1892, the Nutcracker was a colossal flop. It’s easy to see why. Loosely based on an 1816 novella in which an old man gives his goddaughter a doll that comes to life and wages war, the ballet limps through an uneven narrative sprinkled with vague stakes, milquetoast heroes, and culturally insensitive motifs. And yet The Nutcracker is now an unshakeable holiday tradition. The ballet (first performed in the United States by San Francisco Ballet in 1944) marks a rite of passage for dancers, a financial lifeline for dance companies, and an annual tradition for audiences. Versions vary from waltzing flowers to Sugar Plums who tap, skate, stomp, shimmy, and even pop & lock. Its musical score is ubiquitous during the holidays. How did this happen? Janine Kovac , former professional ballet dancer and author of The Nutcracker Chronicles: A Fairytale Memoir, sits down with Shanthi Sekaran ( Lucky Boy, Boomi’s Boombox ) to discuss how this iconic ballet found its footing from artistic debacle to pop culture mainstay, and how it persists in entertaining even the most cynical holiday Scrooges. Janine Kovac writes about power dynamics and women's bodies. A professional ballet dancer whose career spanned over twelve years, Janine danced with companies in San Francisco, Seattle, Iceland, Italy, and in her hometown of El Paso, Texas. Her most recent work of narrative nonfiction The Nutcracker Chronicles: A Fairytale Memoir recently received The Eyelands "Writer's Choice" Award, Greece's International Book Prize. Janine is an alumna of Hedgebrook, MacDowell, and The Mesa Refuge. She is the co-director of Litquake's Lit Crawl and curates Grotto Night for the San Francisco Public Library. Shanthi Sekaran is a novelist and television writer. Her most recent adult novel, Lucky Boy, was named a Best Book of 2017 by NPR, Barnes & Noble, and the San Francisco Chronicle. In 2021, she published her middle grade debut, The Samosa Rebellion, which won the Northern California Book Award and was named an Amazon Editor’s Pick for readers aged 9-13. Her second middle grade novel, Boomi’s Boombox , was a finalist for the California Book Award. She recently wrapped up work on the acclaimed NBC medical drama, New Amsterdam, and this spring, she'll be a Lurie Visiting Author at San Jose State University.

Loosely based on an 1816 novella in which an old man gives his goddaughter a doll that comes to life and wages war, the ballet limps through an uneven narrative sprinkled with vague stakes, milquetoast heroes, and culturally insensitive motifs. And yet The Nutcracker is now an unshakeable holiday tradition. The ballet (first performed in the United States by San Francisco Ballet in 1944) marks a rite of passage for dancers, a financial lifeline for dance companies, and an annual tradition for audiences. Versions vary from waltzing flowers to Sugar Plums who tap, skate, stomp, shimmy, and even pop & lock. Its musical score is ubiquitous during the holidays. How did this happen? Join Janine Kovac , former professional ballet dancer and author of The Nutcracker Chronicles , and Shanthi Sekaran ( Lucky Boy, Boomi’s Boombox ) as they discuss how this iconic ballet found its footing from artistic debacle to pop culture mainstay, and how it persists in entertaining even the most cynical holiday Scrooges. Janine Kovac writes about power dynamics and women's bodies. A professional ballet dancer whose career spanned over twelve years, Janine danced with companies in San Francisco, Seattle, Iceland, Italy, and in her hometown of El Paso, Texas. Her most recent work of narrative nonfiction The Nutcracker Chronicles: A Fairytale Memoir recently received The Eyelands "Writer's Choice" Award, Greece's International Book Prize. Janine is an alumna of Hedgebrook, MacDowell, and The Mesa Refuge. She is the co-director of Litquake's Lit Crawl and curates Grotto Night for the San Francisco Public Library. Shanthi Sekaran is a novelist and television writer. Her most recent adult novel, Lucky Boy, was named a Best Book of 2017 by NPR, Barnes & Noble, and the San Francisco Chronicle. In 2021, she published her middle grade debut, The Samosa Rebellion, which won the Northern California Book Award and was named an Amazon Editor’s Pick for readers aged 9-13. Her second middle grade novel, Boomi’s Boombox , was a finalist for the California Book Award. She recently wrapped up work on the acclaimed NBC medical drama, New Amsterdam, and this spring, she'll be a Lurie Visiting Author at San Jose State University.

0031d2e7-fd8d-4d6f-aa81-e422fbb16b7c: In this deeply experiential yoga practice, we will explore the dynamic interplay between stability and mobility, strength and relaxation, movement and stillness. Through mindful movement, standing and seated practices, breath, and attention to the subtle ways we organize ourselves in space, we'll investigate what allows us to feel both grounded and free. This event happens each week at the Alembic. Rather than striving for perfect alignment or mastering difficult poses, we'll approach the practice as an exploration. We'll slow down enough to notice, experiment with different possibilities, and discover how the balance between effort and ease can change our experience of movement — and of ourselves.. Teacher Bio: Vickie Russell Bell has been teaching yoga for more than 30 years, bringing together the precision of alignment-based yoga with a deep curiosity about how we inhabit our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, and move through the world. She is an E-RYT 500 and Certified Yoga Therapist (C-IAYT), and has studied with some of the most respected teachers in the Iyengar-influenced yoga tradition. Her teaching is grounded in the belief that yoga is less about mastering poses than developing a more intimate relationship with ourselves. Her classes invite students to slow down, pay attention, and explore the constantly shifting relationships between stability and mobility, strength and softness, effort and ease. She teaches students of all ages and abilities, with a particular interest in yoga as a practice for living fully and well over time.
f1965f6a-fbde-4018-9b39-36bd1b1b0ec8: Every Tuesday morning, the Alembic opens for a half-day of silent meditation practice. This is an unguided silent retreat consisting of three 40-minute meditation periods. There will be no teacher-led instruction during the meditation periods. Participants are invited to bring and engage in their own silent meditation practice. Whether you practice mindfulness, Zen, Vipassana, contemplation, prayer, or another silent form of meditation, all are welcome. The retreat begins promptly at 9:30 AM and concludes at 11:50 AM. Please arrive between 9:15 AM and 9:25 AM to remove your shoes, settle in, and find a seat before the first bell. The morning is divided into three periods of silent meditation: 9:30 AM – 10:10 AM 10:20 AM – 11:00 AM 11:10 AM – 11:50 AM A bell will signal the beginning and end of each meditation period. The meditation hall (Sol) is reserved for silent practice during sitting periods. Between sits, participants may quietly stretch, visit the restroom, or spend time in the tearoom. Conversation is permitted during breaks; however, we encourage participants to keep voices low, as some attendees choose to observe silence throughout the entire morning. You are welcome to leave the meditation hall at any time if needed. If you leave during a meditation period, please wait until the next break before re-entering. We ask that all entrances and exits be as quiet and unobtrusive as possible. This is a “Bring Your Own Silent Meditation” retreat. We provide the structure and the space; you provide your own silent practice. Participants may choose to sit in Sol or engage in quiet movement practice in the tearoom during meditation periods. To minimize disruption, please enter Sol only during the transition periods between sits. If you arrive after a meditation period has begun, you are welcome to practice elsewhere in the Alembic until the next bell. The suggested donation is $10. No one will be turned away for lack of funds. We do ask that all attendees register through the Momence app or via the registration link on the Alembic website. Please note that the retreat ends at 11:50 AM, and we ask all participants to depart by 12:00 PM so that our volunteer teacher and staff may close the space in a timely manner. Thank you for helping us maintain a quiet and supportive environment for practice.

1a182e64-fbd7-43ef-a8c0-d9875c5626ed: What is Bookagami? Book Folding is a global art genre. No glue, no scissors, no stress! Learn how to repurpose discarded (or favorite) books into beautiful, sculptural art with the award-winning Marin artist Adrienne Biggs, the originator behind Bookagami. This hands-on Bookagami workshop guides participants through the meditative and mindful practice of folding books into unique, creative, and sustainable art. Adrienne Biggs’ Bookagami art has captivated Marin . A 30-year Marin resident and former book publishing professional, Adrienne will introduce her unique approach—combining origami, altered books, and circular economy principles—to help every attendee fold up to three books into works of art. Workshop Highlights: Learn Bookagami techniques: Start with simple folds and progress to more complex forms, suitable for all skill levels. Embrace sustainability: Discover how book folding diverts unwanted books from the landfill and gives them renewed purpose. Connect and create: Enjoy a community atmosphere where creativity sparks joy and every fold is intentional yet also spontaneous. Take home your art: Finish the session with your handmade Bookagami sculptures to display at home or give as gifts, and the skills to keep folding. What to bring to the workshop: Newer paperbacks or hardcovers with minimum 1” spine (around 300 pages) work best. Books with words and books with images produce different results/color patterns, so you are encouraged to bring and try both at the workshop (see images below for examples). Book Passage can also supply you with books if needed. Meet Your Instructor Adrienne Biggs is an accomplished artist known for fostering creative inclinations within this community, while rescuing books from landfill (or a dusty bookshelf) by repurposing these common two-dimensional objects into three-dimensional works of art that people of all ages can enjoy, create, and share. Since 2024, she has created more than 600 unique “Bookagami” (as she calls them). Her Atlas, 1963: You Are Here won First Place Blue Ribbon at the 2024 Marin County Fair, and her Bug-a-Gami totem and her Stars, Stripes & Stories piece each won ribbons in 2025 and 2026. Past public art exhibits include two-month shows at Town Books in San Anselmo and at Marelli’s in downtown San Rafael; three month shows at the downtown San Rafael Public Library and at the Friends School in San Francisco; one-month show at ACCI Gallery in Berkeley; and various exhibits at ArtWorks Downtown in San Rafael. Her current solo show, Black White & Read All Over, is at Falkirk Cultural Center in San Rafael November 6 - December 15, 2026. Learn more at @IntoTheFoldBookagami on Instagram. She told fun stories and was very motivating. I had three great examples I created and brought home...I am not crafty and Bookagami was easy to do and fun to learn." Diana S.

683c59f8-a899-49a9-9a4b-c9cace076086: Who Gets to Tell the Story? · Every book on a shelf is the result of a series of choices. Which ideas are considered urgent? Which voices are given space? Who decides what gets published, how a book is positioned, who is imagined as its reader, and, ultimately, which books find their way into our hands? From the outside, publishing can look like a relatively straightforward journey: an idea becomes a manuscript, a manuscript becomes a book, a book arrives on a shelf. But behind that journey is an ecosystem of editors, publishers, marketers, distributors, booksellers, institutions, economics, relationships, taste, timing, and power. At every stage, someone is deciding what is worth paying attention to. Join us at Clio’s for a conversation about the politics of publishing with Tim McKee , Publisher of North Atlantic Books; Michelle Phan , Marketing Manager at University of California Press; author and advocate Kelechi Ubozoh ; and cultural anthropologist and Clio’s founding member Cari Borja , whose programming explores what can happen when different voices, disciplines, and ways of knowing are deliberately juxtaposed, creating the possibility for unlikely conversations. Together, we’ll follow a book from idea to bookshelf while asking the harder questions beneath that journey: Who gets through the door? What kinds of knowledge are valued? Which stories enter the cultural conversation, and which don’t? What gets changed, or lost along the way? And what roles do authors, publishers, marketers, booksellers, programmers, and readers play in determining which ideas circulate through our culture? Kelechi Ubozoh’s We’ve Been Too Patient: Voices from Radical Mental Health gives us a particularly powerful book through which to examine these questions. Bringing together voices challenging conventional understandings of mental health and healing, the anthology asks what happens when lived experience itself becomes a form of knowledge, and what it takes for voices outside dominant systems to make their way into print and into public conversation. A bookstore is never simply a place where books are sold. It is a place where voices are chosen, ideas are juxtaposed, unlikely conversations begin, and culture is made. Tim McKee, Publisher, North Atlantic Books Tim came to NAB in 2013 and is honored to serve as publisher. Born in New York City, McKee grew up in Los Angeles and received a BA from Princeton University and an MA in journalism from the University of Missouri. He has worked in the nonprofit sector for his entire career, including serving as the long-time managing editor of The Sun magazine, the grants director for a social-justice foundation in San Francisco, and as a writer for several community-based organizations in California. He has also taught college-level writing and journalism. His book No More Strangers Now: Young Voices from a New South Africa (Dorling Kindersley) was an Honor Book for the Jane Addams Book Award and a Los Angeles Times bestseller. He is happiest when bringing necessary stories to the page. Michelle Phan , Marketing Manager, UC Press Michelle launched her publishing career at North Atlantic Books as a publicist before transitioning to marketing at UC Press. With 7+ years of experience in book promotion, she is passionate about uplifting authors and books that share the knowledge necessary for our times. As Vice President of Bay Area Women in Publishing and Co-Chair of the Robin Seaman Award Committee, she also cares deeply about fostering meaningful relationships and building inclusive community within the industry. Kelechi Ubozoh, Author and advocate For over a decade, Kelechi has worked in the California mental health system in the areas of research and advocacy, community engagement, stigma reduction, youth development and peer support. Kelechi has spoken publicly about her experiences on multiple platforms, including CBS This Morning with Gayle King, O The Oprah Magazine, and The S Word documentary. Kelechi began her career as an investigative reporter in New York City, and was the first student-reporter ever published in The New York Times . In 2019, Kelechi published her anthology with L.D. Green, We’ve Been Too Patien t, which features diverse voices who all share their stories of radical healing and consider the recent movement towards reform in the mental health field, including the mad pride/consumer movement, theater as therapy, peer support, combating stigma, and trauma-informed care. Most recently, she co-authored What I Wish My People Had Known: The Psychiatric Green Book: A Guide for Black Folks with Yolo Akili Robinson, a strategic guide helping Black communities protect against racialized violence and institutional harm.

The Flying Death tells the story of how a modern-day miracle drug was born out of an Amazonian blowgun poison thanks to the efforts of a motley crew of fortune-seeking adventurers—a crew that included a handful of unscrupulous medical researchers, an obsessive White Russian émigré, and an American storyteller with big dreams.”—John Lee Anderson, author of Che: A Revolutionary Life Matt will be joined in conversation by Rebecca Herman, Associate Professor of History, U.C. Berkeley. In The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon (FSG; November 10, 2026), historian Matt O’Hara tells the story of a young, frail American explorer named Richard Gill, who traveled to the Amazon in the 1930s to open a tourist ranch. Instead, he stirred up an international hunt to harvest a local vine known as curare. As Gill and his rivals quickly realized, curare was both a dangerous poison used by local tribes in blow darts and a potential cure for numerous ailments, including multiple sclerosis and other motor diseases. Seeking to treat his own degenerative illness and make a fortune, Gill established connections with tribal leaders and pharmaceutical companies back home—even as his Russian-born rival, Boris Krukoff, sought to do the same. Navigating treacherous terrain and politics, Gill and Krukoff successfully created a veritable curare industrial complex. The plant became a key element in shock therapy treatments and, eventually, in anesthesia back in the United States. Gill and Krukoff’s rivalry and ethical compromises offer a timeless reflection on how personal ambition, competition, and obsession can shape—and sometimes distort—scientific and cultural progress. In this ethnobotanical adventure story, O’Hara deftly explores the intersections of indigenous knowledge, scientific exploration, and exploitation, and poses searching moral ​conundrums about the price of progress. And who pays it. “The Flying Death is as gripping as the exotic poison at its heart. Matt O’Hara is a master researcher who brews a tale at the frontiers of scientific discovery, with healthy doses of ambition and adventure mixed in. This is historical narrative nonfiction at its best.” —Mitchell Zuckoff, author of Lost in Shangri-La “Matt O’Hara has uncovered the thrilling true story of Richard Gill, a sickly American explorer who ventured into the Amazon in 1938—and ended up transforming medicine. Moving from jungle rivers and poison-masters to medical trials and corporate boardrooms, O’Hara offers a gripping, exciting, and deeply researched adventure story about ambition, exploitation, and the true cost of medical breakthroughs.”—Charles Duhigg, author of The Power of Habit “The Flying Death, Matt O’Hara’s brilliant tale of the South American poison curare, is a wild ride driven by courage, mystery, pharmaceutical wrongdoing, and Indigenous wisdom. The story will surprise you, infuriate you—and it will definitely make you smarter.” —Deborah Blum, author of The Poisoner’s Handbook “An unforgettable tale of medicine, ambition, greed, and the natural world, The Flying Death is a true page-turner. Matt O’Hara is a tenacious historian who writes with great skill and with a keen eye for human drama and injustice.”—Hector Tobar, author of Deep Down Dark Matt O’Hara is a professor of history at the University of California, Santa Cruz. He is the award-winning author of many journal articles and two books, The History of the Future in Colonial Mexico and A Flock Divided: Race, Religion, and Politics in Mexico, 1749–1857. Rebecca Herman is Associate Professor of History at UC Berkeley, where she teaches about environmental politics, US-Latin American relations, and modern Latin America. She is the author of Cooperating with the Colossus: A Social and Political History of US Military Bases in World War II Latin America and is currently at work on a book about anti-extractivism in Antarctica. 84e94840-8832-435a-b360-38f6bb59f6ee: A group meditation/authentic relating practice that explores what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to each other Welcome to a twice-monthly drop-in Relatefulness practice with Josh Rosenberg and Daniel Ricciardelli. Relatefulness is an exploration of what is coming up in the present moment as we relate to the others in the group. It is a close friend of relational practices like Circling™, Authentic Relating, and T-Group, with slightly more emphasis on group interaction and flexibility in how to express what is arising in the present moment. This is a mixed-levels event. Beginners are welcome and will be supported with tools to aid their exploration. Advanced practitioners will be challenged to find the next edge of their practice. We cap attendance for the event at 15 people. If you want to be sure to be able to join, purchase your ticket in advance! What We’ll Explore Through paired, small group, and full group processes, we will practice: Noticing and naming the content of our experience, including: our emotions, body sensations, and present moment reactions to others in the group. Noticing and naming the context of our experience, including: our assumptions, the norms of the group, and projections onto one another and society. Revealing our experience to one another to help all of us see each other and our broader social reality more clearly. Leading the group in the direction we want to go. This is a practice where all participants are invited to notice their desires for the group and to practice directing the group by embodying the kinds of expression they want to see more of. Why Come? You may be looking to: Cultivate more authentic, nourishing relationships, where you can be yourself and stay connected. Take your insights about personal growth and explore them in an interpersonal context. Set clear, compassionate boundaries instead of repeating painful patterns This practice helps to develop skills that support all of the above. Also, it's fun! What Not to Expect This is not a therapy session or group healing experience, although healing can occur. It’s a group exploration of what is arising in the present moment. This naturally tends to bring out more truth and love in the group, but there is not a particular goal or endpoint we are trying to reach. Here’s what NOT to expect: A space free of conflict or triggers. When people are open about what's coming up in their experience, things can get edgy sometimes! We don’t view being triggered as inherently negative, but rather a natural part of the human experience that can be rich to explore. We aim for a space where safety grows from honesty and genuine care, not from avoiding interpersonal conflict. To support this, we will establish some boundaries up front, such as asking for explicit consent before making physical contact with others. No enforced hierarchy of emotions. Beauty, awkwardness, boredom, anger, and joy are all welcome. Each experience has worth, and none automatically justify themselves as more important. Expression without attunement. We value honest expression, and we also stay attentive to its impact on others. This is a space for mindful connection, not expression at any cost. Facilitators may pause or redirect moments that move away from relational presence. Other logistics and notes Participants enter the space at 6:30 and we close the doors for the event at 6:35. Please arrive on time! We hope to see you at a future event! Feel free to reach out to jhrosenberg [at] gmail [dot] com or dbricciardelli [at] gmail [dot] com if you have questions about whether this event is a fit for you. More about the facilitators Josh Rosenberg (he/him) is a certified facilitator through the Relateful Company training program. He has hosted and facilitated weekly relatefulness sessions for small groups for several years while continuing to grow his practice through retreats and regularly engaging other facilitators. Josh loves exploring what's honestly coming up in the present moment in a group of people, and the novelty and relief it tends to bring. When he's not leading relatefulness sessions or at work, you may find him loving the heck out of music, movies, and comedy, participating in Michael Taft's meditation courses, or passionately following the New York Jets football team despite its many flaws. In his day job, Josh is CEO at the Forecasting Research Institute, a nonprofit aiming to advance the science of forecasting and increase its policy-relevance. Daniel Ricciardelli (he/him) has hundreds of hours in relational awareness practices of various forms, and is a certified Relatefulness practitioner through the Relateful Company. He draws from a decade of experience guiding men’s circles, performance dance teams, applied AI research, and meditation. Some recent inspirations of his are Ego Development Theory, madhyamaka philosophy, and Brazilian zouk. He is known for his steady, compassionate presence and calibrated relational risk-taking. He works full-time at the intersection of mental health and AI as a machine learning researcher.

dcc20cb4-5e89-435a-8082-257a70c19d6c: UC Berkeley School of Law Professor, Saira Mohamed will discuss her book, WHAT A COUNTRY OWES ITS SOLDIERS . A clarion call to recognize soldiers’ rights, arguing that volunteering to fight and die for one’s country does not mean consenting to exploitation in the process. American leaders endlessly profess their admiration for military service members. But these effusive declarations hardly comport with reality. Soldiers receive shoddy equipment and inadequate medical care; they are ordered to commit crimes and deployed to illegal wars. Such treatment is rarely recognized for what it is: a violation of the duty owed to soldiers by their government. When American service members are injured or killed during training, for example, they and their families are barred from suing the military for negligence or malfeasance. And when the torture of detainees at Abu Ghraib came to light, the subsequent proceedings focused just on low-ranking perpetrators. The psychological harm done to the soldiers themselves by commanders who ordered them to commit torture in the first place went unacknowledged. 745c0337-933d-4cf7-b9cc-c39b376661c3: Three time GRAMMY® winning ensemble · Spanish Harlem Orchestra, the three-time GRAMMY® winning Salsa and Latin Jazz band, sets the gold standard for excellence in authentic, New York-style, hardcore salsa. Whether in a concert hall or at an outdoor jazz festival, there is no easing you in as they come at you full force, from start to finish. Their energy on stage and their rich sound and musical precision leave audiences mesmerized until the last note is played. With an unwavering respect for the music’s storied history, the ensemble’s thirteen world-class musicians and vocalists come together to create an unparalleled musical experience. For over 20 years, SHO has been dedicated to the sounds of the barrio (Spanish Harlem, NYC). Their music is characterized by the raw, organic, and vintage sound defined by the genre. They are on a mission to keep the musical legacy of salsa dura (hard salsa) alive and expand its audience to those who love great music, not just Latin music. Grounded in the past, while focused on the future, they strive to keep the music relevant, creating a unique and fresh approach. “As a leader and producer, my mission and vision are to represent the great history and legacy of this music that I’ve been blessed to be a part of my entire life,” reflects Hernández. “Our passion and commitment to this music is never-ending.” With this unyielding motivation, SHO’s GRAMMY® nominated 2022 release Imágenes Latinas saw the band exploring new dimensions but never deviating from its core belief. “As with all the new SHO recordings, the concept and sound are the same, but the playing of new songs, arrangements, and performances always aim to create a new magic for the listeners,” Hernández adds. SHO released their 9th studio album, Swing Forever , in 2024, further solidifying the group as “the leading light of the salsa reconstruction movement” ( Newsday ). With eight albums and six GRAMMY® nominations, this powerhouse orchestra is aware that it is crucial to continually push itself and raise the bar. Their sixth album, entitled Anniversary, won the 2019 GRAMMY® Award for Best Tropical Album.

4d3c6add-a153-431c-af92-04b5e4dd81d4: Embodiment Practices is an invitation to practice giving ourselves permission to arrive fully to where we are, and gently explore movement and stillness to care for our bodies and ourselves. This event happens each week at the Alembic. As an element of self attunement, we will practice making intuitive choices through a lens of self love, meaning that we are each making choices that are nourishing and responsive to ourselves as individuals in that moment. Part of this practice includes being very intentional and explicit about what kinds of choices we might consider, and being curious about how it feels to try them. There will be many options provided throughout, with guidance around how to navigate choice making, including if this is new to you or you are navigating a limitation or injury. There will be a corner of the room set aside in case you’d like to opt out of the facilitated structure and take a moment for yourself to rest. Opening Circle: We'll ground and check-in with whatever feels present for each of us. We get to welcome ourselves to come as we are. Warm Up: We'll do a guided, full-bodied warm up, tuning the instruments of our bodies and attention, giving ourselves time to shake it out, stretch, wiggle, and move through whatever feels stuck. Movements will be simple enough to follow along, giving us a chance to get out of our heads and drop into our bodies, regulating our nervous system. Drawing on contemporary dance and yoga, there will be flow, rhythm, and music. Movement Explorations: We'll explore movements that deepen our connection with our bodies and our intuition, focusing on concepts and areas of the body that can help us settle and release. Meditation: Finally, we'll settle into meditation and rest. Finding stillness might be sitting/standing/lying down and might include cozy props, having eyes open or closed, and suggestions to make yourself comfortable, including allowing some body movement within that quiet space. Please bring clothes you feel comfortable to move in. It’s recommended to bring long sleeves, long pants and socks with you, in case we are moving on the floor. Bring a journal if you’d like. About Suzanne (Zan): With three decades of contemporary/modern dance experience and 15 years of teaching, Suzanne Beahrs guides students in exploring movement as a pathway to deeper connection—with ourselves, our surroundings, and each other. Her classes blend technical training, creative expression, and guidance on being intentional with how we are each practicing. Her movement style was described by The New York Times as “grounded, silken.” In addition to contemporary dance, she is currently heavily influenced by house dance, contact improvisation, and mindfulness practices. She is currently on faculty at Shawl-Anderson Dance Center and teaches around the Bay Area, including ODC, the Berkeley Alembic, and Finnish Hall. Zan has previously taught extensively at Gibney, Elon University, ADF studios, and many more. She has shown her choreography in NY, NC, CA, AZ, MA, and MO, and performed in works by Ishika Seth, Mo Miner, and others. Beyond the studio, Suzanne is a facilitator and has worked as a DEI consultant. She also enjoys exploring writing, visual art, nature, music, and belonging. Education: MFA in Dance, NYU Tisch School of the Arts; BA in Geology, UC Berkeley Learn more about Suzanne, upcoming classes/workshops (contemporary, embodiment, improvisation, contact improvisation and private lessons): IG @suzannebeahrs suzannebeahrs.com

1b7ee649-72cd-44b0-911d-3c00e6324630: From a stunning new voice in popular science, Bogland is a beguiling debut that invites us to discover the hidden power of Earth’s mysterious landscapes while calling for their defense before it’s too late. Not quite land and not quite water, boglands have long been dismissed as wastelands—too sodden to farm, too perilous to cross, too unruly to be considered beautiful. Come closer, however, and a strange truth emerges: These wild, eerie landscapes stretch our minds, hold the history of humanity, and will shape the future of our planet. In Bogland , acclaimed ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky invites readers to discover the elusive magic and surprising power of these misunderstood places, where the boundaries blur between life and death, past and present, refuge and peril. Venturing from the boreal forests of Canada to the jungles of Borneo, and from the planet’s oldest bog in Greece to some of its newest in Greenland, Turetsky unveils bogs as marvelous paradoxes that defy categorization and their own systemic undervaluation. Here, radical life forms—acid-flinging mosses, amphibian-eating plants—spring from layers upon layers of dead matter. The past and present commingle with uncanny intimacy as peat safeguards artifacts for centuries, along with ancient lives unearthed later as “bog bodies” so remarkably preserved they are sometimes mistaken for the recently missing. Proverbially dangerous, bogs have offered shelter throughout history to the marginalized and resistance movements from Virginia to Vietnam. Crucially, they also regulate the planet’s climate, sequestering nearly one-third of Earth’s soil carbon while covering just 3 percent of its surface—even as accelerating exploitation risks transforming them from climate allies to climate foes, and erasing these ecosystems just as we’re learning to appreciate them. The debut of an extraordinary nature writer, Bogland is an ode and a call to action: to defend bogs’ strangeness and stillness from rising destruction, to value them precisely for their refusal to conform, and to learn from them new ways to adapt, endure, and belong on our changing planet—before it’s too late. Merritt R. Turetsky is a university professor and ecologist. She has served as a science adviser for Eos Magazine and has been featured in Time Magazine and on CNN, PBS NewsHour, and the BBC. She lives in Boulder, Colorado. Ed Yong is the author of two prize-winning New York Times bestsellers, An Immense World and I Contain Multitudes . He won a Pulitzer Prize and a George Polk Award in 2021 for his coverage of the Covid-19 pandemic, and was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024. His work has appeared in many publications including The Atlantic , The New York Times , National Geographic , Wired , and The New Yorker ; he was also featured in three editions of the Best American Science and Nature Writing anthology, which he then guest-edited in 2021. He regularly does talks and interviews, and his TED talk on mind-controlling parasites has been watched by over 1.9 million people. He lives in Oakland, California, with his wife Liz Neeley, founder of Liminal Creations, and his corgi, Typo. He is almost certainly looking at birds right now. Merritt R. 8848a309-94e3-4030-9afb-27702c39793a: Local author Leah Steinberg and legendary Bay Area Author/Historian/DJ Rickey Vincent discuss Steinberg's new book about influential funk drummer Clyde Stubblefield, one of the most-heard but still astonishingly little-known musicians in popular music! During his lifetime Clyde Stubblefield changed the rhythms and sound of music. Finding his start in the segregated city and musical streets of Chattanooga, Tennessee, Stubblefield became the underappreciated source of the funk rhythm that powered the legendary success of James Brown. After six years of playing with the Godfather of Soul, however, Stubblefield had had enough. In 1970, Stubblefield settled down in Madison, Wisconsin, where he could be found playing funk, jazz, R&B, blues, rock and roll, Tex-Mex, and country music for almost anyone who asked. There he found a welcoming and appreciative community of musicians and admirers for the final forty-six years of his life. It was in Madison where Steinberg first met Clyde, befriended him, and asked to write the story of how Stubblefield became the most sampled drummer of all time and how the rhythms of the funky drummer emerged as the foundational sound of hip-hop—despite minimal recognition and compensation.

1fa5ca2f-f6cc-4743-a00c-942b3b841721: Throwin’ Bo’s presents: Storefront Church Storefront Church is the project of Lukas Frank, who's drummed in Phoebe Bridgers' band and appeared on her albums, and the first song of his debut album As We Pass features DIIV frontman Cole Smith, but neither of those affiliations really prepares you for what to expect from As We Pass. It's a 9-song collection that's largely made up of bluesy, gothy, emo-y melancholic songs that sometimes sound like a cross between '90s Cure deep cuts and Nirvana Unplugged. (Lukas also cites Scott Walker as an influence, and you can hear that too.) Most of the album is bare-bones and somber, but Lukas also revs things up for the noise punk of "Faction from Under the Grove," and that fits right in too. With As We Pass, Lukas enters a long, line of depressive singer/songwriters, but even with over half a century of music like this, something about Lukas stands out. He grips you right off the bat with album opener "After the Alphabets" -- the kind of song that can make you drop everything and listen as soon as his voice comes in -- and the album stays that compelling throughout. Even with connections to established artists and the great Sargent House label behind him, this doesn't feel like the smash arrival of a hot new buzz artist; it's the subtle arrival of a songwriter whose songs creep up on you and knock you out when you're least expecting it. Usually, that's even better. Bandcamp | IG Support to be announced. DOORS at 7:00PM | MUSIC at 8:00 PM Tickets

Hiromi will be in Japan February 1-21 but will resume classes when she gets back Hiromi Vardy is a certified Zen Shiatsu, Yang style Tai Chi, and Zhineng Qigong healer and practitioner. She first encountered Tai Chi in 1973 while studying theater design and performance art in London. Initially drawn to the beauty of the movements, she soon discovered that the practice had a profound effect on her consciousness, awakening a deep interest in the healing arts. While collaborating on stage with dancers in London, Hiromi began treating injuries in overworked bodies. In 1976, after a serious accident that resulted in loss of circulation in her leg and concern about possible amputation, she turned to daily Tai Chi practice, self-massage, and treatment from a Japanese acupuncturist. This experience became a turning point in her healing journey and led her back to Japan, where she studied Shiatsu at the Namikoshi School and trained at the Zen Shiatsu Center under Shizuto Masunaga. After moving to the United States with her family in 1987, Hiromi continued deepening her practice and teaching. During a period of significant stress later in her life, she encountered Master Ming Tong Gu and began studying Zhineng (wisdom healing) Qigong under his guidance, eventually becoming licensed to teach. The healing shift she experienced through this practice was profound and continues to inform her teaching today. Since 2013, Hiromi has been dedicated to teaching Zhineng Qigong, expanding her offerings to include online classes in 2020. Her work invites students to explore the foundations of Qigong and Tai Chi as embodied, healing practices that cultivate awareness, vitality, and resilience.

0544dd7f-19b2-4230-a740-4366e6e56aaa: Earl Fontainelle is a historian of ideas who specializes in the cross-over of religion, philosophy, and magic in the ancient world. As listeners to his cult podcast The Secret History of Western Esotericism know, Earl brings a funny, articulate, and good-humored enthusiasm to the esoteric topics he covers. Tonight he is going to offer a mind-expanding view of Platonism, arguing that this key philosophical tradition was also a practice — a path of cultivating altered states of consciousness that approach the cosmic and even psychedelic (at least in spirit, as far as the evidence suggests). Although Plato had no word for ‘consciousness’, his thought pointed towards the vibrant territory where modes of mental experience and features of Being are revealed to be two incomplete ways of describing supreme reality. As Earl will show, in lecture and in conversation with Erik Davis, Platonism continues to shape the way we all frame the question of consciousness to ourselves, whether we know it or not. TEACHER BIOS: Earl Fontainelle is a historian of ideas specializing in the thought-worlds belonging to the first millennium of our era. He produces the Secret History of Western Esotericism Podcast (www.shwep.net), a long-form academic-outreach investigation of the esoteric in western thought from its very beginnings. Erik Davis, PhD, is an author, award-winning journalist, and teacher based in San Francisco. His wide-ranging work focuses on alternative religion, media culture, the popular imagination, and the psychedelic underground. He is the author of High Weirdness: Drugs, Esoterica, and Visionary Experience in the Seventies (2019); Nomad Codes: Adventures in Modern Esoterica (2010); The Visionary State: A Journey through California’s Spiritual Landscape (2006), a critical volume on Led Zeppelin (2005), and the celebrated cult classic TechGnosis: Myth, Magic, and Mysticism in the Age of Information (1998), which remains in print. Davis’s scholarly and popular essays on music, technoculture, drugs, and spirituality have appeared in scores of books, magazines, and journals, and his writing has been translated into a dozen languages. Davis has spoken widely at universities, conferences, retreat centers, and festivals, and has been interviewed by CNN, the BBC, NPR, and the New York Times. He graduated from Yale University in 1988, and earned his PhD in religious studies at Rice University in 2015. He writes the online publication the Burning Shore (www.burningshore.com), and his next book is Blotter: the Untold Story of an Acid Medium (2024).www.techgnosis.com
07783702-7c5e-40b1-a0a7-792668035b21: When we gather with others, conversation almost automatically drifts toward what has already happened or what might happen next. Stories, plans, reactions, hopes—these patterns are so ingrained that we barely notice how completely we relate to one another through the lens of the past and future. But when we pause those habits, something surprising occurs. The room changes. Attention sharpens. A different kind of connection begins to emerge. A small clearing inside awareness opens—a place where no future is rehearsing itself, and no echoes of the past are allowed to enter. We can touch this space alone in contemplative practices, but it's rare to enter it with others. The Present Moment Game is a simple social meditation designed to explore that possibility. Participants speak only from what is happening in the moment, and gently bring each other back when attention drifts. What unfolds is often unexpected, and never the same twice. Curious? Come play! ___________ What to Expect 6:30 PM — Doors open Arrive anytime in the next 30 minutes. You’re welcome to enjoy tea as you settle in—just note that drinks won’t be brought into the circle, so come early if you’d like to enjoy an unrushed cup. 7:00 PM — The event begins This is a “sealed-container” experience. Out of care for the group, we can’t allow late entry, so please be sure to arrive between 6:30 and 7:00. After a brief grace period, doors will close at 7:05. 7:06 PM — Welcome, introductions & game rules A short orientation covering the simple guidelines. 7:25 PM — The Present Moment Game begins 8:25 PM — The game ends We’ll then move into group reflections. ~8:45 PM — Event concludes ___________ Is This Event for You? A few things to consider before you decide: Phones and watches off As an invitation to loosen your grip on time, you’ll be asked to remove your watch and fully power down your phone for the full duration of the experience. This is not an Authentic Relating practice T-Group, Circling, and other AR forms use present-moment awareness as a vehicle for relational exploration. That’s not what we’re doing here. Our subject isn’t each other, but the moment itself. Kindness is essential Please come willing to encounter everyone in the room with openness and warmth. This is a gentle space for contemplation and focused attention, not edge-pushing or confrontation. ___________ One participant’s experience: "As a person who loves, thinks and talks about language for a living, I am wide-eyed at how speaking solely in the present tense feels rich, alive and vital. It’s the best of meditation and conversation, distilled into an hour of social elixir; a stop-you-in-your-tracks nexus of collective mind. I feel hooked, thirsty for more. Alli creates a magical container. You won’t regret it." — Sophia ___________ About your host Alli Magidsohn is the creator of The Present Moment Game, an experimental social meditation that invites a small group to do something surprisingly rare: be fully present together, in real time. The idea grew out of Alli's experience with T-Group, a practice she found genuinely transformative. But as she went deeper, she became increasingly captivated by something specific: the quality of attention that arises when a group of people focus on what's actually happening, right now. That observation became a question: What if the present moment wasn’t just the context of a relationally-focused experience, but the primary subject of the inquiry itself? Drawing in part on the linguistic principles of E-Prime, she designed a set of simple constraints that gently guide conversation away from the past and future, and into the living moment. The result is something playful, quietly profound, and hard to describe until you experience it.
